title: AP Chemistry Independent Foundation Study Library
description: An original text-first nine-chapter study library paired with the internal AP Chemistry foundation pilot. It supports retrieval, calculation setup, model analysis, and evidence-based feedback without reproducing protected course or assessment content.

officialFrameworkTopicSource.cedLabel: AP Chemistry Course and Exam Description, Effective Fall 2024
officialFrameworkTopicSource.note: Public framework topic numbering only; no CED prose, titles, or learning objectives are reproduced.

blueprint.cedEffectiveLabel: Fall 2024 Course Framework V.1; current public reference reviewed 2026-08-20.
blueprint.officialSectionOne: 60 multiple-choice questions in 90 minutes; 50% of the official exam score.
blueprint.officialSectionTwo: 7 free-response questions in 105 minutes; 50% of the official exam score.
blueprint.pilotAlignment: 700-item internal foundation sampler across nine official units; 140 five-item banks; six chemistry science practices; five layered practice angles; data-interpretation, argumentation, model-translation, and method-design synthesis; text-first chapters; no FRQ scoring or laboratory competency claim.

bigIdeas.label: Structure of Matter
bigIdeas.description: Atoms and molecules have structures that determine how they interact and transform.

bigIdeas.label: Properties of Matter
bigIdeas.description: Chemical and physical properties emerge from interactions among particles.

bigIdeas.label: Chemical Reactions
bigIdeas.description: Chemical reactions involve rearrangements of atoms and changes in energy and matter.

bigIdeas.label: Kinetics
bigIdeas.description: Reaction rates depend on molecular collisions, pathways, and energy barriers.

bigIdeas.label: Thermodynamics
bigIdeas.description: Energy changes and entropy help determine the favorability of processes.

bigIdeas.label: Equilibrium
bigIdeas.description: Reversible processes reach dynamic balances described by quantitative relationships.

bigIdeas.label: Acids and Bases
bigIdeas.description: Proton-transfer equilibria and aqueous structure explain acid-base behavior.

sciencePractices.label: Models and Representations
sciencePractices.description: Create, interpret, and translate among particle, symbolic, mathematical, and graphical models.

sciencePractices.label: Question and Method
sciencePractices.description: Design investigations, identify variables and controls, and evaluate methods for chemical questions.

sciencePractices.label: Representing Data and Phenomena
sciencePractices.description: Represent and describe chemical observations, data patterns, and changes at multiple scales.

sciencePractices.label: Model Analysis
sciencePractices.description: Analyze models, assumptions, limitations, and changes in chemical systems.

sciencePractices.label: Mathematical Routines
sciencePractices.description: Apply quantitative relationships, units, proportional reasoning, and chemical calculations.

sciencePractices.label: Argumentation
sciencePractices.description: Make and justify claims with chemical evidence, principles, and logical reasoning.

workedExample.prompt: A mass spectrum of gallium shows Ga-69 (68.926 amu, 60.11%) and Ga-71 (70.925 amu, 39.89%). Calculate gallium's average atomic mass and explain why it lies closer to 69 than to 71.
steps: Step 1: Convert percent abundances to decimal fractions: 0.6011 for Ga-69 and 0.3989 for Ga-71.
Step 3: The weighted average (69.72 amu) matches the periodic table and falls closer to 69 because Ga-69 accounts for roughly 60% of naturally occurring atoms.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students often take a simple unweighted arithmetic mean of isotope masses without multiplying each mass by its fractional abundance.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Weight every isotope mass by its decimal abundance from the mass spectrum and verify that the final atomic mass leans toward the most abundant peak.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners frequently treat an empirical formula obtained from percent-composition data as the true molecular formula of a covalent compound.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Divide the experimentally measured molar mass by the empirical formula mass to find the integer multiplier needed for the molecular formula.

sections.heading: Atomic structure and electron configuration
sections.content: The quantum model places electrons in shells and subshells of increasing energy. Electron configurations fill lower-energy subshells first, and the outermost, or valence, electrons determine most chemical behavior. Coulomb’s law explains the pattern: an electron is held more strongly when it is closer to the nucleus and when the effective nuclear charge it experiences is larger. Photoelectron spectroscopy measures the energy needed to remove electrons from each subshell; the position of a peak reports binding energy and the relative height reports how many electrons occupy that subshell, so a spectrum is direct evidence for shell structure.

workedExample.prompt: A photoelectron spectrum of a neutral atom has five peaks with relative heights 2, 2, 6, 2, and 3 from highest to lowest binding energy. Identify the element and compare its 1s binding energy to oxygen.
steps: Step 1: Assign subshells from highest binding energy (closest to nucleus) outward: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³, totaling 15 electrons, which identifies phosphorus (P).
Step 2: Compare nuclear charges using Coulomb's law (F ∝ q1q2/r²): phosphorus has +15 protons versus +8 protons in oxygen.
Step 3: Greater nuclear attraction pulls phosphorus's 1s electrons tighter to the nucleus, so its 1s peak appears at a much higher binding energy than oxygen's 1s.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students routinely read PES horizontal axes left-to-right as increasing binding energy even when AP plots reverse the axis.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Always inspect the PES axis numbers first; core 1s electrons appear at the highest binding energy (often on the left), and peak height indicates electron count.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners often remove 3d electrons before 4s electrons when writing configurations for transition-metal cations like Fe2+.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Transition metals lose outermost valence s electrons before inner d electrons, so Fe ([Ar]4s²3d⁶) ionizes to Fe2+ as [Ar]3d⁶.

sections.heading: Periodic trends and valence electrons
sections.content: Periodic trends follow from electron configuration and Coulomb’s law. Across a period, effective nuclear charge rises while the outer shell stays the same, so atomic radius decreases and ionization energy and electronegativity generally increase. Down a group, added shells place valence electrons farther out and more shielded, so radius increases and ionization energy decreases. Ions follow the same logic: cations are smaller than their parent atoms and anions are larger. Elements in the same group share valence electron counts and therefore similar reactivity and typical ionic charges, which is why the periodic table predicts formulas and properties.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why oxygen (IE1 = 1,314 kJ/mol) has a lower first ionization energy than nitrogen (IE1 = 1,402 kJ/mol) even though oxygen has a larger nuclear charge and smaller atomic radius.
steps: Step 1: Compare valence orbital occupancies: nitrogen is 2s²2p³ (three unpaired 2p electrons), whereas oxygen is 2s²2p⁴ (one paired 2p orbital and two unpaired).
Step 2: In oxygen, placing two electrons in the same 2p orbital introduces extra electron-electron repulsion within that shared spatial region.
Step 3: This pairing repulsion slightly offsets oxygen's higher effective nuclear charge, making its fourth 2p electron easier to remove than nitrogen's unpaired 2p electron.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students often justify periodic trends on AP FRQs merely by restating periodic table position ("further right means smaller").
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Always explain periodic trends using atomic structure and Coulomb's law: cite effective nuclear charge across a period and added energy shells (shielding) down a group.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes assume isoelectronic species like O2−, F−, Na+, and Mg2+ share the same radius because they have 10 electrons.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Within an isoelectronic series, identical electron shielding means radius shrinks steadily as proton count increases (O2− > F− > Na+ > Mg2+).

workedExample.prompt: Compare resonance structures for the cyanate ion (OCN−) using formal charge to identify the dominant Lewis structure, then predict its molecular geometry and central-atom hybridization.
steps: Step 1: Count 16 valence electrons (6 + 4 + 5 + 1) and evaluate two low-charge resonance forms: [:O=C=N:]− (FC: O=0, C=0, N=−1) and [:O−C≡N:]− (FC: O=−1, C=0, N=0).
Step 2: Both structures minimize formal charge magnitudes, but :O−C≡N: places the −1 formal charge on the more electronegative oxygen atom, making it the major contributor.
Step 3: Central carbon has two electron domains and zero lone pairs, yielding sp hybridization and a linear molecular geometry (180° bond angle).

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students often report electron-domain geometry as molecular geometry, for example labeling NH3 or H2O as tetrahedral.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Count all domains to find electron geometry, then name molecular shape from bonded atom positions alone (NH3 is trigonal pyramidal; H2O is bent).

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners frequently assume any molecule containing polar covalent bonds must be a polar molecule overall.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Evaluate 3D vector symmetry first; identical polar bonds cancel completely in symmetric geometries such as linear CO2, trigonal planar BF3, and tetrahedral CCl4.

sections.heading: Types of bonds and bond energy
sections.content: Bond type depends on the electronegativity of the atoms involved. Large differences give ionic bonds in which electrons transfer and ions attract; small differences give covalent bonds in which electrons are shared, polar when the sharing is unequal. Metals bond through a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalized electrons. A covalent bond forms because the potential energy of the atoms is lowest at a particular separation: too close and the nuclei repel, too far and the attraction weakens. workedExample.prompt: Compare the potential-energy curves of N2 (triple bond, 110 pm, 945 kJ/mol) and O2 (double bond, 121 pm, 498 kJ/mol). Locate each energy minimum and explain the difference in well depth and position.

sections.heading: Ionic and metallic solids, and alloys
sections.content: In an ionic solid, cations and anions occupy a repeating lattice held by electrostatic attraction in every direction. Lattice energy grows with ion charge and shrinks as ion size increases, which explains high melting points and brittleness: shifting the lattice brings like charges together and it fractures. Ionic solids conduct only when melted or dissolved, when the ions are free to move. Metals are lattices of cations surrounded by delocalized electrons, which makes them conductive, malleable, and ductile because layers can slide without breaking bonds. Alloys are mixtures of metals; substitutional alloys replace some atoms with others of similar size, and interstitial alloys fit small atoms into the gaps, typically making the material harder.

workedExample.prompt: Magnesium oxide (MgO, mp 2,852°C) melts far higher than sodium fluoride (NaF, mp 993°C) despite comparable internuclear distances (210 pm vs 231 pm). Justify this difference using Coulomb's law.
steps: Step 1: Identify ionic charges in each lattice: MgO contains Mg2+ and O2− (|q1·q2| = 4), whereas NaF contains Na+ and F− (|q1·q2| = 1).
Step 2: By Coulomb's law (E ∝ q1q2/r), the 4-fold greater charge product and slightly smaller interionic spacing produce roughly four times stronger electrostatic attraction in MgO.
Step 3: Overcoming MgO's much higher lattice energy requires far greater thermal kinetic energy, explaining its dramatically higher melting point.

misconceptionGuidance.repair: Electrical conduction requires mobile charge carriers; ions locked in a solid crystal cannot move until the salt is melted or dissolved in water.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners frequently confuse substitutional alloys with interstitial alloys when explaining changes in metal malleability and density.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Substitutional alloys replace host atoms with similar-sized metals (brass), whereas interstitial alloys insert tiny atoms like carbon into lattice gaps (steel) to restrict slip.

workedExample.prompt: Ethanol (CH3CH2OH, bp 78°C) and dimethyl ether (CH3OCH3, bp −24°C) share the molar mass 46.07 g/mol. Identify all intermolecular forces in each liquid and account for ethanol's higher boiling point.
steps: Step 1: Both isomers have identical molar masses and similar electron cloud sizes, giving comparable London dispersion forces alongside dipole-dipole attractions.
Step 2: Ethanol contains a polarized O−H bond that forms strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds between molecules, whereas dimethyl ether lacks H bonded to O, N, or F.
Step 3: Separating ethanol molecules into the gas phase requires breaking those hydrogen bonds, producing a 102°C higher boiling point and lower vapor pressure.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes assume hydrogen-bonding molecules always boil higher than nonpolar molecules regardless of molecular size.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Large polarizable electron clouds generate very strong London dispersion forces, explaining why nonpolar I2 is a solid at room temperature while H2O is a liquid.

sections.heading: Gases: the ideal gas law and kinetic molecular theory
sections.content: The ideal gas law, PV equals nRT, relates pressure, volume, amount, and temperature for a gas whose particles are treated as points that do not attract one another. Kinetic molecular theory supplies the picture: particles move randomly, collisions with the walls create pressure, and average kinetic energy depends only on temperature, so at a given temperature lighter particles move faster. Dalton’s law gives the total pressure of a mixture as the sum of partial pressures. Real gases deviate from ideal behavior at high pressure, where particle volume matters, and at low temperature, where attractions slow particles and lower the pressure below the ideal prediction.

workedExample.prompt: A rigid 4.00 L flask at 298 K holds 0.200 mol He and 0.300 mol N2. Compute total pressure and partial pressure of N2, then compare both gases in average kinetic energy and molecular speed.
steps: Step 1: Sum gas moles (n_tot = 0.500 mol) and apply PV = nRT: P_tot = (0.500 mol)(0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K))(298 K) / 4.00 L = 3.06 atm.
Step 2: Use Dalton's law with mole fraction X_N2 = 0.300 / 0.500 = 0.600: P_N2 = 0.600 × 3.057 atm = 1.83 atm.
Step 3: At equal temperature (298 K), He and N2 share identical average kinetic energy, while lighter He (4.00 vs 28.01 g/mol) moves with a much higher average speed.

sections.heading: Solutions, separations, and spectroscopy
sections.content: A solution is a homogeneous mixture whose composition is expressed as molarity, moles of solute per liter of solution. Particle-level pictures show solvent molecules surrounding dissolved ions or molecules; solubility depends on whether solute-solvent attractions compete with the attractions each had before mixing, which is why polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents. Mixtures are separated by exploiting differences in properties: distillation uses boiling points, chromatography uses differing attraction to a stationary phase, and filtration uses particle size. Light interacts with matter in ways that identify and quantify substances: different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum excite electronic, vibrational, or rotational changes, the photoelectric effect shows that light delivers energy in quanta proportional to frequency, and the Beer-Lambert law relates absorbance to concentration and path length.

workedExample.prompt: A 0.040 M CuSO4 standard gives absorbance A = 0.48 at 635 nm in a 1.00 cm cuvette. Find molar absorptivity ε, compute the concentration of an unknown with A = 0.30, and predict the effect of water droplets in the cuvette.
steps: Step 1: Rearrange Beer-Lambert law (A = εbc) to solve for molar absorptivity: ε = 0.48 / (1.00 cm × 0.040 M) = 12 M⁻¹·cm⁻¹.
Step 2: Calculate the unknown concentration using the same path length and wavelength: c = A / (εb) = 0.30 / (12 × 1.00) = 0.025 M.
Step 3: Residual distilled water droplets inside the cuvette dilute the unknown solution, decreasing its actual concentration and causing an artificially low absorbance reading.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students sometimes measure spectrophotometric absorbance at a random wavelength rather than selecting the analyte's maximum absorbance wavelength.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Choosing λ_max maximizes sensitivity and ensures a flat absorbance region where slight wavelength drift causes minimal deviation from Beer-Lambert linearity.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners frequently mix up which electromagnetic region drives electronic transitions versus molecular vibrations or rotations.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: UV-visible light excites electronic transitions, infrared radiation excites covalent bond vibrations, and lower-energy microwaves excite molecular rotations.

workedExample.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation when 50.0 mL of 0.20 M Pb(NO3)2(aq) mixes with 50.0 mL of 0.40 M KI(aq) to precipitate PbI2(s), and identify all ions remaining in the filtrate.
steps: Step 1: Dissociate soluble strong electrolytes into aqueous ions: Pb2+ + 2 NO3− + 2 K+ + 2 I− → PbI2(s) + 2 K+ + 2 NO3−.
Step 2: Cancel spectator ions (K+ and NO3−) to obtain the net ionic equation: Pb2+(aq) + 2 I−(aq) → PbI2(s).
Step 3: Check stoichiometry: 0.010 mol Pb2+ reacts completely with 0.020 mol I−, leaving only 0.020 mol K+(aq) and 0.020 mol NO3−(aq) dissolved in the 100.0 mL filtrate.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students often keep soluble spectator ions inside net ionic equations or leave strong electrolytes written as intact molecular formulas.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Dissociate all soluble strong electrolytes first, then cancel ions that appear identically on both sides so only chemically reacting species remain.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes split insoluble precipitates, weak acids like HF, or pure liquids like H2O(l) into separate ions in net ionic equations.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Only soluble strong acids, strong bases, and soluble ionic salts dissociate into ions; keep precipitates, weak electrolytes, gases, and pure liquids intact.

sections.heading: Stoichiometry and titration
sections.content: A balanced equation gives mole ratios between reactants and products, and stoichiometry uses those ratios with molar masses and molarities to convert between masses, moles, volumes of solution, and volumes of gas. When reactants are not present in the exact ratio, the limiting reactant is consumed first and sets the maximum product; the other reactant is in excess. Percent yield compares the actual amount obtained to that theoretical maximum. Titration applies stoichiometry to solutions: a solution of known concentration is added to one of unknown concentration until an indicator or a measurement shows the equivalence point, where the moles of titrant match the stoichiometric requirement.

workedExample.prompt: In 2 Al(s) + 3 Cl2(g) → 2 AlCl3(s), 5.40 g Al (26.98 g/mol) reacts with 14.2 g Cl2 (70.90 g/mol). Identify the limiting reactant and calculate the theoretical yield of AlCl3 (133.34 g/mol) in grams.
steps: Step 1: Convert reactant masses to moles: n(Al) = 5.40 / 26.98 = 0.200 mol Al; n(Cl2) = 14.2 / 70.90 = 0.2003 mol Cl2.
Step 2: Calculate AlCl3 moles each could form: Al gives 0.200 × (2/2) = 0.200 mol, while Cl2 gives 0.2003 × (2/3) = 0.1335 mol, so Cl2 is limiting.
Step 3: Convert limiting product moles to grams: 0.1335 mol × 133.34 g/mol = 17.8 g AlCl3 theoretical yield.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students routinely assume the reactant with the smaller starting mass in grams must be the limiting reactant.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Always convert masses to moles and divide by stoichiometric coefficients (or compute product moles from each) because molar masses and mole ratios govern consumption.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes think a titration equivalence point occurs whenever equal volumes of titrant and analyte have been mixed.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Equivalence occurs when titrant and analyte reach their exact balanced mole ratio, which yields equal volumes only if concentrations and coefficients match.

sections.heading: Reaction types: acid-base and redox
sections.content: Chemical reactions are classified by what is transferred or rearranged. Precipitation reactions form an insoluble product from dissolved ions. Acid-base reactions transfer a proton from a Brønsted-Lowry acid to a base; strong acids and bases dissociate completely in water and weak ones only partially. Oxidation-reduction reactions transfer electrons: the species that loses electrons is oxidized and is the reducing agent, and the species that gains them is reduced and is the oxidizing agent. Oxidation numbers track electrons through a reaction, and half-reactions show the oxidation and reduction separately so that electrons balance when they are combined.

workedExample.prompt: Balance MnO4−(aq) + Fe2+(aq) → Mn2+(aq) + Fe3+(aq) in acidic solution via half-reactions, and identify which species is oxidized and which acts as the oxidizing agent.

sections.heading: Collision model and reaction energy profiles
sections.content: An elementary reaction happens in a single step, and its rate law follows directly from its molecularity: a unimolecular step is first order and a bimolecular step is second order overall. The collision model explains why: reaction requires particles to collide with enough energy to overcome the activation barrier and with a suitable orientation. Raising temperature increases the fraction of collisions with sufficient energy, which is why rates rise steeply with temperature. A reaction energy profile plots potential energy along the reaction coordinate; the peak is the transition state, the height of the peak above the reactants is the activation energy, and the difference between products and reactants is the overall energy change.

workedExample.prompt: First-order decomposition of N2O5 at 45°C has a half-life of 20.0 min. Calculate k and the fraction remaining after 60.0 min, then use the collision model to explain why heating increases k.
steps: Step 1: Compute the first-order rate constant from half-life: k = ln(2) / t_1/2 = 0.693 / 20.0 min = 0.0347 min⁻¹.
Step 2: Recognize that 60.0 min equals 3 half-lives (60.0 / 20.0), so the fraction remaining is (1/2)³ = 1/8 = 0.125 (12.5%).
Step 3: Raising temperature shifts the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution rightward, dramatically increasing the fraction of collisions with energy ≥ Ea and increasing k.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students often explain faster reaction rates at higher temperature mainly by citing more frequent collisions rather than activation energy.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: While collision frequency rises modestly with T, the dominant kinetic effect is an exponential increase in the fraction of collisions possessing energy ≥ Ea.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes assume every reaction has a constant concentration-independent half-life like radioactive decay.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Constant half-life is unique to first-order kinetics; second-order half-life (1/(k[A]0)) doubles each time concentration halves, while zero-order half-life shrinks.

sections.heading: Reaction mechanisms and catalysis
sections.content: A mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps that adds up to the overall reaction. Species that appear in one step and are consumed in a later one are intermediates; they never appear in the overall equation. The slowest step, the rate-determining step, controls the rate, and a proposed mechanism must give a rate law consistent with experiment. When the slow step follows a fast equilibrium, intermediates in its rate law are replaced using the equilibrium relationship. A multistep reaction has an energy profile with one peak per step and valleys for intermediates. A catalyst provides a different pathway with lower activation energy; it is consumed in one step and regenerated in another, so it appears in the mechanism but not in the overall equation, and it does not change the position of equilibrium.

workedExample.prompt: Given the mechanism Step 1 (fast eq): 2 NO ⇌ N2O2 and Step 2 (slow): N2O2 + O2 → 2 NO2, identify the intermediate, derive the rate law in terms of reactants, and describe how a catalyst alters the energy profile.

workedExample.prompt: Mixing 50.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl with 50.0 mL of 1.00 M NaOH (100.0 g total, c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)) raises temperature from 22.0°C to 28.7°C. Calculate ΔH_rxn in kJ/mol of H2O produced.
steps: Step 1: Calculate heat absorbed by the aqueous solution: q_soln = mcΔT = (100.0 g)(4.18 J/(g·°C))(28.7 − 22.0°C) = +2,801 J = +2.80 kJ.
Step 2: Apply conservation of energy to the reaction system: q_rxn = −q_soln = −2.80 kJ (exothermic heat release).
Step 3: Divide by moles of water formed (0.0500 L × 1.00 M = 0.0500 mol): ΔH_rxn = −2.80 kJ / 0.0500 mol = −56.0 kJ/mol.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students routinely report a positive ΔH when solution temperature rises in a coffee-cup calorimeter because ΔT is positive.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes divide q_rxn by the sum of both reactant moles rather than the moles of limiting reactant or reaction extent.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Always normalize ΔH_rxn per mole of limiting reactant consumed (or per mole of product matching the balanced equation stoichiometry).

sections.heading: Calorimetry and the energy of phase changes
sections.content: Heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of an object by one kelvin, and specific heat capacity is the same quantity per gram. The heat transferred in a temperature change is the mass times the specific heat times the temperature change, q equals mcΔT. Calorimetry measures the energy change of a process from the temperature change of a known mass of water or of a calorimeter, assuming energy is conserved between the system and its surroundings. During a phase change the temperature stays constant while energy goes into overcoming intermolecular attractions, so the energy of melting or vaporizing is the amount per mole times the amount of substance and does not involve ΔT. A heating curve shows sloped segments for temperature changes and flat segments for phase changes.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate total heat needed to convert 36.0 g of ice (2.00 mol H2O) at 0.0°C to liquid water at 25.0°C (ΔH_fus = 6.01 kJ/mol, c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), and explain why temperature stays flat while melting.
steps: Step 1: Compute phase-change energy for melting at 0.0°C: q1 = n·ΔH_fus = (2.00 mol)(6.01 kJ/mol) = 12.02 kJ.
Step 2: Compute warming energy from 0.0°C to 25.0°C: q2 = mcΔT = (36.0 g)(4.18 J/(g·°C))(25.0°C) = 3,762 J = 3.76 kJ.
Step 3: Sum segments (q_tot = 12.02 + 3.76 = 15.8 kJ); temperature stays flat during melting because absorbed heat disrupts H-bonds (potential energy) rather than raising kinetic energy.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students often attempt to plug ΔT = 0 into q = mcΔT during a melting or boiling plateau and mistakenly conclude zero heat is transferred.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes assume temperature stops rising on a heating curve because the heat source was turned off.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Heat continues entering steadily along a plateau, but that energy increases particle potential energy by overcoming intermolecular attractions instead of molecular speed.

sections.heading: Enthalpy of reaction: bond enthalpies, formation, and Hess’s law
sections.content: The enthalpy change of a reaction is the energy transferred as heat at constant pressure, negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions, and it scales with the amount of reaction that occurs. It can be estimated from bond enthalpies: energy is required to break the bonds in the reactants and released when the bonds in the products form, so ΔH is approximately the sum of bonds broken minus the sum of bonds formed. It can be calculated exactly from standard enthalpies of formation as the sum for products minus the sum for reactants, because the formation enthalpy of an element in its standard state is zero. Hess’s law states that enthalpy is a state function, so the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in several, which lets known reactions be combined to find an unknown one.

workedExample.prompt: Estimate ΔH°_rxn for H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2 HCl(g) using bond enthalpies (H−H = 436, Cl−Cl = 243, H−Cl = 431 kJ/mol), and justify why the reaction is exothermic from bond strengths.
steps: Step 1: Sum endothermic energy needed to break reactant bonds: Σ(broken) = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ/mol.
Step 2: Sum exothermic energy released by forming product bonds: Σ(formed) = 2 × 431 = 862 kJ/mol.
Step 3: Compute ΔH°_rxn = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed) = 679 − 862 = −183 kJ/mol; forming two strong H−Cl bonds releases more energy than breaking H−H and Cl−Cl absorbs.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students frequently apply products minus reactants to bond enthalpies just like enthalpies of formation, flipping the sign of ΔH.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Use products minus reactants for ΔH°_f, but use Σ(bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bonds formed in products) for bond enthalpies because breaking is positive.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners often flip or multiply target equations in Hess's law without reversing the sign or scaling the corresponding ΔH values.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Track every algebraic manipulation explicitly: reversing an equation negates ΔH, and multiplying stoichiometric coefficients multiplies ΔH by the same factor.

workedExample.prompt: At equilibrium, N2(g) + 3 H2(g) ⇌ 2 NH3(g) (ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol) is compressed to half its volume at fixed temperature. Use Q vs K to predict the shift, and contrast this with heating the vessel.
steps: Step 1: Halving volume doubles all molarities, so Q = (2[NH3])² / [(2[N2])(2[H2])³] = (4/16)K = 0.25 K, giving Q < K.
Step 2: Because Q < K, the forward rate exceeds the reverse rate and the mixture shifts right toward fewer gas moles (4 → 2) until Q equals unchanged K.
Step 3: In contrast, raising temperature favors the endothermic reverse direction (shifts left) and decreases the numerical value of K itself.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students routinely state that reactant and product concentrations become equal once a chemical system reaches dynamic equilibrium.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: At equilibrium, forward and reverse reaction rates are equal while concentrations remain constant at whatever ratio satisfies K (rarely equal).

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners often claim that adding a catalyst or injecting an inert gas at constant volume shifts equilibrium position toward products.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: A catalyst accelerates both forward and reverse rates equally without altering Q or K, and inert gas at fixed volume leaves all reacting partial pressures unchanged.

sections.heading: Calculating and interpreting the equilibrium constant
sections.content: The equilibrium constant K is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, each raised to its coefficient, with pure solids and liquids omitted. A very large K means the reaction goes nearly to completion and a very small K means it barely proceeds; a K near 1 means substantial amounts of both remain. K depends only on temperature. Reversing a reaction takes the reciprocal of K, multiplying coefficients raises K to that power, and adding reactions multiplies their constants. An ICE table organizes initial concentrations, the change in terms of a single variable, and the equilibrium concentrations so that K can be calculated or equilibrium amounts predicted; when K is very small the change is often negligible compared with the initial amount, which simplifies the algebra. workedExample.prompt: A 1.00 L flask initially contains 0.500 M H2(g) and 0.500 M I2(g) at 448°C where Kc = 49.0 for H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g). Use an ICE table to calculate equilibrium concentrations of all three gases.
steps: Step 1: Set up ICE equilibrium terms: [H2] = 0.500 − x, [I2] = 0.500 − x, and [HI] = 2x, giving Kc = (2x)² / (0.500 − x)² = 49.0.
Step 2: Take the square root of both sides: 2x / (0.500 − x) = 7.00, so 2x = 3.50 − 7x, yielding 9x = 3.50 and x = 0.389 M.
Step 3: Substitute x back: [H2] = [I2] = 0.111 M and [HI] = 0.778 M; verify (0.778)² / (0.111)² = 49.1 ≈ 49.0.

sections.heading: Solubility equilibria and the common-ion effect
sections.content: A sparingly soluble ionic solid establishes an equilibrium with its dissolved ions, described by the solubility product Ksp, which is the product of the ion concentrations raised to their coefficients. Ksp can be found from a measured solubility and, in reverse, molar solubility can be calculated from Ksp using the stoichiometry of dissolution. Comparing the ion product Q with Ksp predicts whether a precipitate forms: if Q exceeds Ksp the solution is supersaturated and solid forms. Adding a solution that already contains one of the ions, the common-ion effect, shifts the equilibrium toward the solid and lowers solubility, exactly as Le Chatelier’s principle predicts.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the molar solubility of AgCl (Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) in pure water and in 0.10 M NaCl(aq), and explain how the common-ion effect alters solubility without changing Ksp.

Step 2: In 0.10 M NaCl, [Cl−] ≈ 0.10 M (since s << 0.10), so 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ = s(0.10), yielding s = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M.
Step 3: Added Cl− makes Q > Ksp initially and shifts dissolution left, cutting solubility over 7,000-fold while Ksp remains constant at fixed temperature.

workedExample.prompt: Calculate the pH and percent ionization of 0.10 M acetic acid (CH3COOH, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), and explain why its pH is significantly higher than that of 0.10 M HCl.
steps: Step 1: Set up Ka = [H3O+][CH3COO−]/[CH3COOH] = x²/(0.10 − x) ≈ x²/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, giving x = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ M.
Step 2: Verify the 5% rule via percent ionization: (1.34 × 10⁻³ / 0.10) × 100% = 1.34% (< 5%, valid).
Step 3: Compute pH = −log(1.34 × 10⁻³) = 2.87; unlike strong acid HCl (100% ionized, pH = 1.00), weak acetic acid remains mostly protonated at equilibrium.

sections.heading: Acid-base titrations and the molecular structure of acids
sections.content: Neutralization between an acid and a base produces water and a salt, and the pH of the resulting solution depends on whether the reactants were strong or weak. A titration curve of pH against volume of titrant reveals this: a strong acid with a strong base gives an equivalence point at pH 7, while a weak acid gives an equivalence point above 7 because its conjugate base remains. For a weak acid, the region before the equivalence point is a buffer, and at the half-equivalence point the pH equals the pKa. Molecular structure explains acid strength: a bond to hydrogen that is more polar or weaker releases the proton more readily, and electronegative atoms near the acidic hydrogen or resonance in the conjugate base stabilize the negative charge and make the acid stronger.

workedExample.prompt: A 25.0 mL sample of 0.100 M formic acid (HCOOH, pKa = 3.74) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. Determine the pH after 12.5 mL NaOH is added, and explain why the 25.0 mL equivalence point has pH > 7.
steps: Step 1: Equivalence requires 2.50 mmol NaOH (25.0 mL), so 12.5 mL is the half-equivalence point where half the HCOOH has converted to HCOO− ([HCOOH] = [HCOO−]).
Step 2: At half-equivalence, Henderson-Hasselbalch gives pH = pKa + log(1) = 3.74; formic acid is stronger than acetic acid because H lacks an electron-donating methyl group.
Step 3: At 25.0 mL equivalence, only conjugate base HCOO− remains, which hydrolyzes water (HCOO− + H2O ⇌ HCOOH + OH−) to generate excess OH− and pH > 7.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students routinely assume every acid-base titration has an equivalence point pH equal to 7.00.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Only strong-acid plus strong-base titrations reach pH 7; weak-acid equivalence points are basic (pH > 7) and weak-base equivalence points are acidic (pH < 7).

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes think oxyacid strength increases with the number of hydrogen atoms rather than with electronegative oxygen atoms.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Additional oxygen atoms withdraw electron density inductively, polarizing the O−H bond and delocalizing negative charge across the conjugate base to raise Ka.

sections.heading: Buffers: pKa, Henderson-Hasselbalch, capacity, and solubility
sections.content: A buffer is a solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base, or a weak base and its conjugate acid, that resists changes in pH. Added acid is consumed by the conjugate base and added base by the weak acid, so the ratio of the two changes only slightly. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH equals pKa plus the logarithm of the base-to-acid ratio, gives the pH of a buffer and shows that pH equals pKa when the two components are equal. A buffer is most effective near its pKa, and its capacity, the amount of acid or base it can absorb, depends on the absolute concentrations of the components. Because pH controls whether an ion is protonated, the solubility of salts of weak acids or bases changes with pH: a salt of a weak acid dissolves more in acidic solution because the anion is removed as the acid forms.

workedExample.prompt: A 1.00 L buffer holds 0.30 mol CH3COOH (pKa = 4.74) and 0.30 mol CH3COO−. Compute the pH after adding 0.05 mol solid NaOH (no volume change), and explain why a 0.03 M/0.03 M buffer fails under this addition.
steps: Step 1: Perform neutralization stoichiometry first: 0.05 mol OH− converts 0.05 mol CH3COOH into CH3COO−, leaving 0.25 mol HA and 0.35 mol A−.
Step 2: Apply Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = 4.74 + log(0.35 / 0.25) = 4.74 + log(1.40) = 4.74 + 0.15 = 4.89.
Step 3: The 0.30 M buffer shifts by only +0.15 pH unit, whereas a 0.03 M buffer has insufficient acid capacity (0.03 < 0.05 mol) and leaves excess strong base.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students often plug added strong acid or base straight into the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation without updating moles by neutralization.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Always run a limiting-reactant stoichiometry step in moles first (OH− consumes HA to make A−; H3O+ consumes A− to make HA), then apply Henderson-Hasselbalch.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes believe two buffers with the same 1:1 [A−]/[HA] ratio have identical buffer capacity regardless of concentration.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: The ratio fixes the initial pH near pKa, whereas total molar concentration of the conjugate pair determines how much acid or base the buffer can absorb.

workedExample.prompt: For CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g), ΔH° = +178 kJ/mol and ΔS° = +161 J/(mol·K). Calculate ΔG° at 298 K, assess favorability, and find the minimum temperature where decomposition becomes favorable.
steps: Step 1: Convert ΔS° into kJ/(mol·K) to match ΔH°: +161 J/(mol·K) = +0.161 kJ/(mol·K).
Step 2: Compute ΔG° at 298 K: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 178 − (298)(0.161) = 178 − 48.0 = +130 kJ/mol (> 0, thermodynamically unfavorable).
Step 3: Set ΔG° = 0 to find crossover T = ΔH°/ΔS° = 178 / 0.161 = 1,106 K (833°C); above 1,106 K, the −TΔS° term dominates and makes ΔG° negative.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students routinely forget to convert ΔS° from J/(mol·K) to kJ/(mol·K) before substituting into ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Check energy units before every Gibbs calculation: divide J/(mol·K) by 1,000 so both ΔH° and TΔS° are expressed consistently in kJ/mol.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners frequently assume any reaction with a negative ΔG° must proceed rapidly as soon as reactants are mixed.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Negative ΔG° establishes thermodynamic favorability only; a high activation energy barrier can still hold the process under kinetic control at room temperature.

sections.heading: Free energy, equilibrium, and coupled reactions
sections.content: A reaction can be thermodynamically favorable yet proceed imperceptibly slowly if its activation energy is large, so favorability and rate are separate questions: thermodynamic control asks whether products are lower in free energy, and kinetic control asks whether the barrier can be crossed. The standard free energy change is related to the equilibrium constant by ΔG° equals −RT ln K, so a negative ΔG° means K is greater than 1 and products are favored at equilibrium, while ΔG° of zero means K equals 1. Under nonstandard conditions the free energy change depends on the reaction quotient and drives the system toward equilibrium from either side. A thermodynamically unfavorable reaction can be made to occur by coupling it to a favorable one that shares an intermediate, so the combined free energy change is negative, which is how cells use the hydrolysis of ATP and how metals are extracted from ores.

workedExample.prompt: A process has ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol at 298 K (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)). Compute its equilibrium constant K, and explain how coupling it to a reaction with ΔG° = +8.2 kJ/mol drives net product formation.
steps: Step 1: Convert ΔG° to −11,400 J/mol and rearrange ΔG° = −RT ln K to get ln K = −(−11,400) / (8.314 × 298) = 11,400 / 2,477.6 = 4.601.
Step 2: Exponentiate to obtain K = e^4.601 ≈ 1.0 × 10² (99.6), confirming a strongly product-favored equilibrium (K > 1).
Step 3: Coupling both steps through a shared intermediate sums free energies to ΔG°_net = −11.4 + 8.2 = −3.2 kJ/mol < 0, rendering the overall sequence favorable.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students often claim that ΔG° equals zero at chemical equilibrium instead of distinguishing standard ΔG° from actual ΔG.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Actual nonstandard ΔG reaches zero at equilibrium (when Q = K), whereas standard ΔG° = −RT ln K equals zero only in the special case where K = 1.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners sometimes pair a negative ΔG° with K < 1 because both contain small or negative-looking signs.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Because ΔG° = −RT ln K carries a leading minus sign, negative ΔG° always means ln K > 0 and K > 1 (products favored), while positive ΔG° means K < 1.

sections.heading: Electrochemical cells and electrolysis
sections.content: An electrochemical cell separates the oxidation and reduction halves of a redox reaction so that electrons flow through an external circuit. In a galvanic cell the reaction is favorable and produces electrical energy: oxidation occurs at the anode, reduction at the cathode, electrons flow from anode to cathode, and a salt bridge keeps the solutions electrically neutral. The standard cell potential is the difference between the standard reduction potentials of the cathode and anode, and a positive potential corresponds to a negative free energy change through ΔG° equals −nFE°. Under nonstandard conditions the cell potential shifts with the reaction quotient and falls to zero at equilibrium. workedExample.prompt: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, E°(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V. Compute E°_cell and ΔG° (F = 96,485 C/mol e−), then find the mass of Cu (63.55 g/mol) plated by 2.00 A flowing for 965 s.
steps: Step 1: Assign Cu2+ reduction to the cathode and Zn oxidation to the anode (n = 2 e−): E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
Step 2: Compute standard free energy: ΔG° = −nFE°_cell = −(2)(96,485 C/mol)(1.10 J/C) = −212,267 J/mol = −212 kJ/mol.
Step 3: Apply Faraday's law: q = It = (2.00 A)(965 s) = 1,930 C → 1,930 / 96,485 = 0.0200 mol e− → 0.0100 mol Cu × 63.55 g/mol = 0.636 g Cu plated.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Students frequently multiply standard reduction potentials E° by stoichiometric coefficients when balancing electron transfer between half-cells.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Voltage is an intensive property (joules per coulomb), so never scale E° by reaction coefficients; instead account for electron count n inside ΔG° = −nFE°.

misconceptionGuidance.misconception: Learners often describe electrons traveling through the aqueous salt bridge to complete the circuit in a galvanic cell.
misconceptionGuidance.repair: Electrons travel exclusively from anode to cathode through the external wire, while anions and cations migrate through the salt bridge to maintain electroneutrality.

Use Q vs. 1 to predict Nernst voltage shifts under nonstandard concentrations, and use charge Q = I t with Faraday constant F for electrolytic stoichiometry.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 1: Atomic Structure and Properties?
flashcards.back: Connect moles, isotopes, electron configurations, and periodic trends to observable chemical properties.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Atomic structure and electron configuration?
flashcards.back: The quantum model places electrons in shells and subshells of increasing energy. Electron configurations fill lower-energy subshells first, and the outermost, or valence, electrons determine most chemical behavior.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Periodic trends and valence electrons?
flashcards.back: Periodic trends follow from electron configuration and Coulomb’s law. Across a period, effective nuclear charge rises while the outer shell stays the same, so atomic radius decreases and ionization energy and electronegativity generally increase.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 2: Compound Structure and Properties?
flashcards.back: Use Lewis, resonance, VSEPR, and bonding-energy models to predict compound structure and behavior.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Types of bonds and bond energy?
flashcards.back: Bond type depends on the electronegativity of the atoms involved. Large differences give ionic bonds in which electrons transfer and ions attract; small differences give covalent bonds in which electrons are shared, polar when the sharing is unequal.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Ionic and metallic solids, and alloys?
flashcards.back: In an ionic solid, cations and anions occupy a repeating lattice held by electrostatic attraction in every direction. Lattice energy grows with ion charge and shrinks as ion size increases, which explains high melting points and brittleness: shifting the lattice brings like charges together and it fractures.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 3: Properties of Substances and Mixtures?
flashcards.back: Translate among particle, mathematical, and macroscopic representations of substances and mixtures.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Gases: the ideal gas law and kinetic molecular theory?
flashcards.back: The ideal gas law, PV equals nRT, relates pressure, volume, amount, and temperature for a gas whose particles are treated as points that do not attract one another. Kinetic molecular theory supplies the picture: particles move randomly, collisions with the walls create pressure, and average kinetic energy depends only on temperature, so at a given temperature lighter particles move faster.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Solutions, separations, and spectroscopy?
flashcards.back: A solution is a homogeneous mixture whose composition is expressed as molarity, moles of solute per liter of solution. Particle-level pictures show solvent molecules surrounding dissolved ions or molecules; solubility depends on whether solute-solvent attractions compete with the attractions each had before mixing, which is why polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 4: Chemical Reactions?
flashcards.back: Balance and interpret reaction equations, net ionic equations, stoichiometric ratios, titrations, and redox changes.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Stoichiometry and titration?
flashcards.back: A balanced equation gives mole ratios between reactants and products, and stoichiometry uses those ratios with molar masses and molarities to convert between masses, moles, volumes of solution, and volumes of gas. When reactants are not present in the exact ratio, the limiting reactant is consumed first and sets the maximum product; the other reactant is in excess.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Reaction types: acid-base and redox?
flashcards.back: Chemical reactions are classified by what is transferred or rearranged. Precipitation reactions form an insoluble product from dissolved ions.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 5: Kinetics?
flashcards.back: Use rate data and energy profiles to infer rate laws, mechanisms, catalysts, and controlling steps.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Collision model and reaction energy profiles?
flashcards.back: An elementary reaction happens in a single step, and its rate law follows directly from its molecularity: a unimolecular step is first order and a bimolecular step is second order overall. The collision model explains why: reaction requires particles to collide with enough energy to overcome the activation barrier and with a suitable orientation.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Reaction mechanisms and catalysis?
flashcards.back: A mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps that adds up to the overall reaction. Species that appear in one step and are consumed in a later one are intermediates; they never appear in the overall equation.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 6: Thermochemistry?
flashcards.back: Calculate and explain heat and enthalpy changes using multiple consistent representations.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Calorimetry and the energy of phase changes?
flashcards.back: Heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of an object by one kelvin, and specific heat capacity is the same quantity per gram. The heat transferred in a temperature change is the mass times the specific heat times the temperature change, q equals mcΔT.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Enthalpy of reaction: bond enthalpies, formation, and Hess’s law?
flashcards.back: The enthalpy change of a reaction is the energy transferred as heat at constant pressure, negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions, and it scales with the amount of reaction that occurs. It can be estimated from bond enthalpies: energy is required to break the bonds in the reactants and released when the bonds in the products form, so ΔH is approximately the sum of bonds broken minus the sum of bonds formed.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 7: Equilibrium?
flashcards.back: Use reaction quotients, equilibrium constants, ICE reasoning, and Le Chatelier models to analyze reversible systems.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Calculating and interpreting the equilibrium constant?
flashcards.back: The equilibrium constant K is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, each raised to its coefficient, with pure solids and liquids omitted. A very large K means the reaction goes nearly to completion and a very small K means it barely proceeds; a K near 1 means substantial amounts of both remain.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Solubility equilibria and the common-ion effect?
flashcards.back: A sparingly soluble ionic solid establishes an equilibrium with its dissolved ions, described by the solubility product Ksp, which is the product of the ion concentrations raised to their coefficients. Ksp can be found from a measured solubility and, in reverse, molar solubility can be calculated from Ksp using the stoichiometry of dissolution.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 8: Acids and Bases?
flashcards.back: Analyze pH, pKa, conjugate pairs, titration regions, buffers, and acid-base solubility effects.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Acid-base titrations and the molecular structure of acids?
flashcards.back: Neutralization between an acid and a base produces water and a salt, and the pH of the resulting solution depends on whether the reactants were strong or weak. A titration curve of pH against volume of titrant reveals this: a strong acid with a strong base gives an equivalence point at pH 7, while a weak acid gives an equivalence point above 7 because its conjugate base remains.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Buffers: pKa, Henderson-Hasselbalch, capacity, and solubility?
flashcards.back: A buffer is a solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base, or a weak base and its conjugate acid, that resists changes in pH. Added acid is consumed by the conjugate base and added base by the weak acid, so the ratio of the two changes only slightly.

flashcards.front: What is the central reasoning move for Unit 9: Thermodynamics and Electrochemistry?
flashcards.back: Use thermodynamic and electrochemical relationships to analyze spontaneity, cell potentials, nonstandard conditions, and electrolysis.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Free energy, equilibrium, and coupled reactions?
flashcards.back: A reaction can be thermodynamically favorable yet proceed imperceptibly slowly if its activation energy is large, so favorability and rate are separate questions: thermodynamic control asks whether products are lower in free energy, and kinetic control asks whether the barrier can be crossed. The standard free energy change is related to the equilibrium constant by ΔG° equals −RT ln K, so a negative ΔG° means K is greater than 1 and products are favored at equilibrium, while ΔG° of zero means K equals 1.

flashcards.front: What key chemical principle and boundary govern Electrochemical cells and electrolysis?
flashcards.back: An electrochemical cell separates the oxidation and reduction halves of a redox reaction so that electrons flow through an external circuit. In a galvanic cell the reaction is favorable and produces electrical energy: oxidation occurs at the anode, reduction at the cathode, electrons flow from anode to cathode, and a salt bridge keeps the solutions electrically neutral.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Identify an element from a photoelectron spectrum
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that uses a photoelectron spectrum to determine an element’s electron configuration, justifies the identification, and predicts one periodic property from it. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic data: A photoelectron spectrum of a neutral atom shows four peaks. In order of decreasing binding energy their relative heights are 2, 2, 6, and 1. The lowest-energy peak sits at a noticeably smaller binding energy than the peak of height 6.
taskParts: Assign each peak to a subshell and write the electron configuration the spectrum supports, explaining how peak height and position were used.
Identify the element and justify the identification from the total electron count and the configuration.
Predict whether this element’s first ionization energy is higher or lower than that of the element immediately before it in the periodic table, and explain using Coulomb’s law.

planningFrame.label: Read
planningFrame.guidance: Match each peak height to an electron count and each position to a shell distance from the nucleus.

planningFrame.label: Configure
planningFrame.guidance: Write the subshells in order of decreasing binding energy and total the electrons.

planningFrame.label: Identify
planningFrame.guidance: Use the electron count of a neutral atom to name the element.

planningFrame.label: Predict
planningFrame.guidance: Compare effective nuclear charge and shell for the property asked, then state the direction.

successCriteria: Peaks are assigned as 1s, 2s, 2p, and 3s with heights matching electron counts of 2, 2, 6, and 1.
The element is identified as sodium from eleven electrons in a neutral atom.
The single 3s electron is recognized as being in a new shell, more shielded and farther from the nucleus.
The ionization energy prediction is lower than neon’s and is justified by shielding and distance, not by mass.
commonPitfalls: Reading a taller peak as a higher binding energy rather than as more electrons.
Placing the 3s electron in the same shell as the 2p electrons because its peak is adjacent.
Identifying the element from the number of peaks instead of the total electron count.
Predicting the ionization trend from atomic mass rather than from effective nuclear charge.
sampleOutline: Configuration: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1 from heights 2, 2, 6, 1 in order of binding energy.
Identity: eleven electrons in a neutral atom, so sodium.
Prediction: the 3s electron is well shielded and far from the nucleus, so first ionization energy is much lower than neon’s.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Predict polarity from a Lewis structure
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that draws a molecule’s Lewis structure, uses geometry to decide whether it is polar, and connects that decision to an observable property. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic scenario: Two compounds have the formulas CF4 and CH2F2. A student measures that CH2F2 has a boiling point about 76 degrees higher than CF4 even though CF4 has the greater molar mass, and asks why.
taskParts: Draw or describe the Lewis structure and molecular geometry of each compound, including the electron-domain arrangement around carbon.
Determine whether each molecule has a net dipole moment and justify the answer from bond polarity and geometry.
Explain the boiling point difference using intermolecular forces, and identify which comparison the molar masses alone would have predicted.

planningFrame.label: Structure
planningFrame.guidance: Count valence electrons, place bonds and lone pairs, and name the electron-domain geometry.

planningFrame.label: Bond dipoles
planningFrame.guidance: Mark each polar bond with its direction from electronegativity differences.

planningFrame.label: Net dipole
planningFrame.guidance: Decide whether the bond dipoles cancel by symmetry or add to a net moment.

planningFrame.label: Property
planningFrame.guidance: Link a net dipole to dipole-dipole forces and to the boiling point, then note what mass alone predicts.

successCriteria: Both molecules are described as tetrahedral around carbon with four bonding domains and no lone pairs on carbon.
CF4 is identified as nonpolar because four equal carbon-fluorine dipoles cancel, and CH2F2 as polar because they do not.
The boiling point difference is attributed to dipole-dipole attractions in CH2F2 in addition to dispersion forces.
The response notes that dispersion forces and molar mass alone would predict the opposite order.
commonPitfalls: Concluding a molecule is polar because it contains polar bonds, without checking geometry.
Describing CH2F2 as having a different electron-domain geometry from CF4.
Attributing the higher boiling point to hydrogen bonding, which CH2F2 cannot form.
Ignoring that CF4 has stronger dispersion forces from its greater electron count.
sampleOutline: Structures: both tetrahedral; CF4 has four identical polar bonds, CH2F2 has two carbon-fluorine and two carbon-hydrogen bonds.
Polarity: CF4 dipoles cancel by symmetry; CH2F2 dipoles reinforce toward the fluorines, giving a net dipole.
Property: dipole-dipole attraction raises the boiling point of CH2F2 above what its smaller dispersion forces would give.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Use a calibration curve and the ideal gas law
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that determines an unknown concentration from absorbance data and then uses gas measurements to find an amount of substance, stating assumptions at each step. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic data: Standard solutions of a blue dye give absorbances of 0.10, 0.20, 0.40, and 0.60 at concentrations of 0.050, 0.100, 0.200, and 0.300 millimolar in a 1.00 cm cell. An unknown solution reads 0.28. Separately, a reaction releases a gas that is collected over water; the collected gas occupies 245 milliliters at 298 kelvin and a total pressure of 101.3 kilopascals, and the vapor pressure of water at that temperature is 3.2 kilopascals.
taskParts: Determine the concentration of the unknown dye solution from the calibration data and state the relationship you relied on.
Calculate the moles of gas collected, showing how the water vapor pressure is handled.
Identify one assumption behind each calculation and describe an observation that would show the assumption had failed.

planningFrame.label: Relationship
planningFrame.guidance: Name the law that links absorbance to concentration and check that the standards are linear.

planningFrame.label: Interpolate
planningFrame.guidance: Find the concentration whose absorbance matches the unknown, staying within the calibrated range.

planningFrame.label: Correct
planningFrame.guidance: Subtract water vapor pressure to get the partial pressure of the collected gas before using the gas law.

planningFrame.label: Assume
planningFrame.guidance: State the ideal-gas and linear-absorbance assumptions and what would violate each.

successCriteria: The unknown is found near 0.14 millimolar by linear interpolation using the Beer-Lambert relationship.
The gas pressure used is 98.1 kilopascals after subtracting water vapor pressure.
The gas calculation gives about 0.0097 moles using consistent units for R, pressure, and volume.
Each assumption is paired with a specific failure sign, such as a curved calibration plot or deviation at high pressure.
commonPitfalls: Using the total pressure without subtracting the water vapor contribution.
Extrapolating the calibration curve beyond the highest standard.
Mixing kilopascals with a value of R expressed in atmospheres.
Stating that absorbance is proportional to concentration without noting the fixed path length and wavelength.
sampleOutline: Dye: absorbance is proportional to concentration; 0.28 falls between 0.20 and 0.40, giving about 0.14 millimolar.
Gas: partial pressure 101.3 minus 3.2 equals 98.1 kilopascals; n equals PV divided by RT, about 0.0097 mol.
Assumptions: linear response within the calibrated range; ideal behavior at near-atmospheric pressure.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Analyze a redox reaction quantitatively
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that balances a redox reaction, identifies the limiting reactant from given amounts, and predicts the observable outcome. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic scenario: A strip of aluminum with mass 0.540 grams is placed in 100.0 milliliters of 0.400 molar copper(II) sulfate solution. The aluminum is oxidized to aluminum ions and copper ions are reduced to copper metal. The solution is initially blue.
taskParts: Write the balanced net ionic equation, identify the species oxidized and reduced, and state the number of electrons transferred per formula unit of reaction.
Determine which reactant is limiting and calculate the mass of copper metal that can form.
Predict what the solution and the strip will look like when the reaction stops, and justify the prediction from the limiting reactant.

planningFrame.label: Half-reactions
planningFrame.guidance: Write the oxidation and reduction halves and balance electrons before combining.

planningFrame.label: Moles
planningFrame.guidance: Convert the aluminum mass and the copper ion solution to moles.

planningFrame.label: Compare
planningFrame.guidance: Use the balanced ratio to find which reactant runs out first.

planningFrame.label: Observe
planningFrame.guidance: Translate the leftover reactant into what would be seen in the beaker.

successCriteria: The net ionic equation is 2 Al + 3 Cu2+ → 2 Al3+ + 3 Cu with six electrons transferred.
Aluminum is 0.0200 mol and copper ions are 0.0400 mol, and aluminum is identified as limiting by the 2 to 3 ratio.
The mass of copper formed is about 1.91 grams from 0.0300 mol of copper produced by limiting aluminum.
The prediction states that the aluminum strip is completely consumed and the solution fades to a lighter blue, because excess copper ions remain.
commonPitfalls: Comparing moles directly without applying the 2 to 3 stoichiometric ratio.
Treating the reactant with fewer moles as limiting without the ratio.
Reporting the electrons per atom of aluminum as the total transferred in the balanced equation.
Predicting the solution turns completely colorless or that aluminum remains when aluminum is the limiting reactant.
sampleOutline: Equation: 2 Al + 3 Cu2+ → 2 Al3+ + 3 Cu; aluminum oxidized, copper ion reduced.
Limiting: 0.0200 mol Al needs 0.0300 mol Cu2+ (leaving 0.0100 mol Cu2+ excess); 0.0400 mol Cu2+ needs 0.0267 mol Al, so Al limits.
Outcome: 0.0300 mol Cu, about 1.91 g; aluminum strip is consumed and solution fades to a lighter blue.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Rate law from data and mechanism
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Derive a rate law and test a mechanism
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that determines a rate law from initial-rate data, then evaluates whether a proposed mechanism is consistent with it. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic data for the reaction 2 NO + O2 → 2 NO2. Trial 1: [NO] 0.010 M, [O2] 0.010 M, rate 2.5 × 10−5 M/s. Trial 2: [NO] 0.020 M, [O2] 0.010 M, rate 1.0 × 10−4 M/s. Trial 3: [NO] 0.010 M, [O2] 0.020 M, rate 5.0 × 10−5 M/s. A proposed mechanism has a fast equilibrium 2 NO ⇌ N2O2 followed by a slow step N2O2 + O2 → 2 NO2.
taskParts: Determine the order with respect to each reactant and write the rate law with the value of the rate constant.
Derive the rate law predicted by the proposed mechanism, explaining how the intermediate is handled.
Decide whether the mechanism is consistent with the data, and state clearly what consistency does and does not prove.

planningFrame.label: Compare
planningFrame.guidance: Change one concentration at a time between trials and read the effect on rate.

planningFrame.label: Rate law
planningFrame.guidance: Write orders as exponents, then solve one trial for k with units.

planningFrame.label: Mechanism
planningFrame.guidance: Write the slow-step rate law, then replace the intermediate using the fast equilibrium.

planningFrame.label: Judge
planningFrame.guidance: Match the derived law to the experimental one and state the limit of that evidence.

successCriteria: The reaction is found to be second order in NO and first order in O2, giving rate equals k[NO]2[O2].
The rate constant is about 25 M−2 s−1, with units derived rather than assumed.
The intermediate N2O2 is replaced using K[NO]2 from the fast equilibrium, giving the same form.
The response states the mechanism is consistent with, but not proven by, the data.
commonPitfalls: Reading the orders from the coefficients of the overall equation.
Leaving the intermediate in the final rate law.
Reporting k without units or with units for the wrong overall order.
Claiming the data prove the mechanism rather than that they fail to rule it out.
sampleOutline: Data: doubling NO quadruples the rate, second order; doubling O2 doubles it, first order.
Rate law: rate equals k[NO]2[O2], k equals 2.5 × 10−5 divided by (0.010)2(0.010), about 25 M−2 s−1.
Mechanism: slow step gives k2[N2O2][O2]; substituting [N2O2] equals K[NO]2 matches the observed form.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Determine an enthalpy change two ways
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that finds a reaction enthalpy from calorimetry data, checks it against a Hess’s law calculation, and explains the difference. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic data: 50.0 milliliters of 1.00 molar hydrochloric acid and 50.0 milliliters of 1.00 molar sodium hydroxide, both at 22.0 degrees Celsius, are mixed in a foam cup. The temperature rises to 28.6 degrees Celsius. Assume the solution has the density and specific heat of water, 1.00 g/mL and 4.18 J/g·K. Separately, standard enthalpies of formation are given: H+(aq) 0, OH−(aq) −230 kJ/mol, H2O(l) −286 kJ/mol.
taskParts: Calculate the heat absorbed by the solution and the enthalpy change per mole of water formed from the calorimetry data.
Calculate the enthalpy change for the neutralization from the enthalpies of formation.
Compare the two values, propose the most likely reason for any difference, and describe how the experiment could be modified to reduce it.

planningFrame.label: Heat
planningFrame.guidance: Use the total solution mass, the specific heat, and the temperature change to find q, then attach the sign for the reaction.

planningFrame.label: Per mole
planningFrame.guidance: Find the moles of water formed from the limiting amounts and divide.

planningFrame.label: Formation
planningFrame.guidance: Apply products minus reactants with the given formation enthalpies.

planningFrame.label: Reconcile
planningFrame.guidance: Attribute a gap to heat lost to the cup or air and name a fix.

successCriteria: q for the solution is about 2,760 joules from 100 g, 4.18 J/g·K, and 6.6 K.
The reaction enthalpy is about −55 kJ per mole of water, negative because the reaction released heat.
The formation calculation gives −56 kJ per mole from −286 minus (0 plus −230).
The difference is attributed to heat absorbed by the cup or lost to the surroundings, and a calorimeter constant or insulation is proposed.
commonPitfalls: Using only 50 g of solution instead of the combined 100 g.
Reporting the enthalpy change as positive when the temperature rose.
Forgetting that the enthalpy of formation of aqueous H+ is defined as zero.
Attributing the gap to measurement error without naming where heat could have gone.
sampleOutline: Calorimetry: q equals 100 g × 4.18 J/g·K × 6.6 K, about 2.76 kJ; 0.0500 mol water formed; ΔH about −55 kJ/mol.
Formation: −286 − (0 + −230) equals −56 kJ/mol.
Reconcile: the calorimeter absorbed some heat; determine its heat capacity or improve insulation.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Calculate equilibrium amounts and predict a shift
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that finds equilibrium concentrations from an initial mixture and an equilibrium constant, then predicts and justifies the direction of change after a disturbance. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic scenario: For the gas-phase reaction A ⇌ 2 B, K is 4.0 × 10−4 at a fixed temperature. A container initially holds 0.500 molar A and no B. After equilibrium is reached, the volume of the container is halved at constant temperature.
taskParts: Set up an ICE table and calculate the equilibrium concentrations of A and B, justifying any approximation used.
Determine the direction the reaction shifts when the volume is halved, using the reaction quotient.
Explain what happens to the value of K during this change and why.

planningFrame.label: Table
planningFrame.guidance: Write initial, change, and equilibrium rows with the change in terms of one variable and the coefficients.

planningFrame.label: Solve
planningFrame.guidance: Write the K expression, decide whether x is small compared with 0.500, and solve.

planningFrame.label: Quotient
planningFrame.guidance: Compute Q immediately after the disturbance and compare it with K.

planningFrame.label: Constant
planningFrame.guidance: State that K depends only on temperature and did not change.

successCriteria: The change row is −x for A and +2x for B, and K equals (2x)2 divided by (0.500 − x).
The small-x approximation is justified because K is small, giving x about 0.0071 and [B] about 0.014 molar.
Halving the volume doubles both concentrations, making Q greater than K, so the reaction shifts toward A.
The response states that K is unchanged because temperature is constant.
commonPitfalls: Writing the change in B as +x rather than +2x.
Using the approximation without checking that x is small relative to the initial concentration.
Claiming the shift is toward more moles of gas when pressure increases.
Saying K changed because the concentrations changed.
sampleOutline: Disturbance: concentrations double, Q = (0.028)2 / 0.986 ≈ 8 × 10−4 > K, so the reaction shifts left toward A.
Constant: K is unchanged; only temperature changes K.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Interpret a weak-acid titration curve
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that extracts an acid’s pKa and concentration from titration data, identifies the buffer region, and calculates the pH at a point within it. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic data: 25.0 milliliters of a weak monoprotic acid is titrated with 0.100 molar sodium hydroxide. The pH is 2.7 at the start, 4.2 after 10.0 milliliters of base, and rises steeply near 20.0 milliliters, reaching 8.4 at the equivalence point. The half-equivalence pH is 4.2.
taskParts: Determine the concentration of the acid from the equivalence volume and the pKa from the half-equivalence point.
Explain why the pH at the equivalence point is above 7, naming the species responsible.
Calculate the pH after 15.0 milliliters of base has been added and explain why this region resists pH change.

planningFrame.label: Equivalence
planningFrame.guidance: Use the moles of base at equivalence to find the moles and concentration of acid.

planningFrame.label: pKa
planningFrame.guidance: Read the pH at half the equivalence volume; that value is the pKa.

planningFrame.label: Species
planningFrame.guidance: Identify what remains in solution at equivalence and whether it is acidic or basic.

planningFrame.label: Buffer
planningFrame.guidance: Find the moles of acid and conjugate base after 15.0 milliliters, then apply Henderson-Hasselbalch.

successCriteria: The acid concentration is 0.0800 molar from 0.00200 mol of base in 25.0 milliliters.
The pKa is 4.2, read at 10.0 milliliters, half the equivalence volume.
The basic equivalence point is attributed to the conjugate base accepting protons from water.
The pH at 15.0 milliliters is about 4.7 from the ratio 3 to 1 of conjugate base to acid.
commonPitfalls: Reading the pKa at the equivalence point instead of the half-equivalence point.
Assuming the equivalence pH is 7 because moles of acid and base are equal.
Using the initial acid concentration in Henderson-Hasselbalch instead of the remaining moles.
Describing the buffer region as having constant pH rather than a slowly changing pH.
sampleOutline: Concentration: 0.0200 L × 0.100 M equals 0.00200 mol acid in 0.0250 L, so 0.0800 M; pKa 4.2 at half-equivalence.
Equivalence: only the conjugate base remains; it is a weak base, so pH 8.4.
Buffer point: 0.00150 mol base formed, 0.00050 mol acid left; pH equals 4.2 plus log 3, about 4.7.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Judge favorability and design a galvanic cell
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan a response that decides whether a reaction is thermodynamically favorable, builds a galvanic cell from it, and relates the cell potential to free energy. This is a planning exercise, not an official AP prompt or scored response.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Original synthetic data: Standard reduction potentials are given as Ag+ + e− → Ag, +0.80 V, and Ni2+ + 2 e− → Ni, −0.25 V. For a separate reaction, ΔH° is −92 kJ/mol and ΔS° is −199 J/mol·K.
taskParts: Determine whether the separate reaction is thermodynamically favorable at 298 kelvin and at 600 kelvin, showing the free-energy reasoning.
Identify the anode, cathode, and overall reaction of a galvanic cell built from the silver and nickel half-reactions, and calculate its standard potential.
Relate the cell potential to the standard free energy change and state what a positive potential implies about K.

planningFrame.label: Free energy
planningFrame.guidance: Compute ΔG° equals ΔH° minus TΔS° at each temperature with consistent units.

planningFrame.label: Cell
planningFrame.guidance: Assign reduction to the more positive potential and oxidation to the other, then balance electrons.

planningFrame.label: Potential
planningFrame.guidance: Subtract the anode reduction potential from the cathode reduction potential without scaling for coefficients.

planningFrame.label: Link
planningFrame.guidance: Use ΔG° equals −nFE° and the sign of ΔG° to infer whether K exceeds 1.

successCriteria: ΔG° is about −33 kJ/mol at 298 kelvin and about +27 kJ/mol at 600 kelvin, so favorability reverses with temperature.
Silver is the cathode and nickel the anode, with overall reaction Ni + 2 Ag+ → Ni2+ + 2 Ag.
The standard cell potential is 1.05 V, with the silver potential not doubled.
A positive potential gives a negative ΔG° through −nFE° with n equal to 2, so K is greater than 1.
commonPitfalls: Mixing kilojoules and joules when combining ΔH° and TΔS°.
Doubling the silver reduction potential because its half-reaction is multiplied by two.
Assigning the anode to the more positive potential.
Concluding that a favorable reaction must also be fast.
sampleOutline: Cell: cathode Ag+/Ag, anode Ni/Ni2+; E° equals 0.80 − (−0.25) equals 1.05 V.
Link: ΔG° equals −2 × 96,485 × 1.05, about −203 kJ, so K is much greater than 1.
