glossary.definition: Spectroscopic method measuring the binding energy needed to eject electrons from gaseous atoms; peak positions reflect subshell Coulombic attraction and relative peak heights directly indicate electron occupancy.

Net positive nuclear attraction (Zeff) experienced by a valence electron after accounting for core-electron shielding, explaining decreasing atomic radius and rising ionization energy across a period.

Minimum energy required to remove one mole of the highest-energy electrons from gaseous ground-state atoms; generally increases across a period with higher Zeff and decreases down a group as distance increases.

One of two or more valid Lewis diagrams differing only in the placement of delocalized pi or lone-pair electrons; the actual species is a single hybrid with identical intermediate bond lengths and bond orders.

Endothermic energy required to break one mole of a specific covalent bond in the gas phase; higher bond order and shorter internuclear bond length yield greater bond strength and larger dissociation energy.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Types of bonds and bond energy

glossary.definition: Electrostatic energy stabilizing an ionic solid relative to separated gaseous ions; grows in magnitude with higher ion charges and smaller ionic radii according to Coulomb’s law, raising melting points.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Ionic and metallic solids, and alloys

glossary.definition: Intermolecular attractions arising from temporary, induced dipoles present in all atoms and molecules; strengthen with larger, more polarizable electron clouds and greater contact surface area.

glossary.definition: Microscopic model explaining ideal gas behavior (PV = nRT) through negligible particle volume, elastic collisions, zero intermolecular attractions, and average kinetic energy proportional solely to Kelvin temperature.

glossary.definition: Quantitative spectroscopic relation (A = εbc) linking solution absorbance (A) linearly to molar absorptivity (ε), cuvette path length (b), and analyte molarity (c) at an optimal wavelength.

occurrences.chapterTitle: Unit 3: Properties of Substances and Mixtures
occurrences.domain: Unit 3: Properties of Substances and Mixtures

glossary.definition: Balanced chemical equation displaying only the ions and molecules directly transformed during an aqueous reaction while canceling unchanged spectator ions that appear identically on both sides.
Reactant consumed completely first according to balanced stoichiometric mole ratios, thereby capping the maximum theoretical yield of product while leaving all other reactants in excess.

Electron-transfer reaction in which the reducing agent is oxidized (loses electrons, increasing oxidation number) while the oxidizing agent is simultaneously reduced (gains electrons, decreasing oxidation number).

Experimentally determined expression (rate = k[A]^m[B]^n) linking reaction rate to reactant concentrations raised to their reaction orders, where the temperature-dependent rate constant k reflects the activation barrier.
Minimum kinetic energy (Ea) that colliding reactant particles must supply in an effective orientation to reach the high-energy transition state and convert into products.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Collision model and reaction energy profiles

glossary.definition: Slowest elementary step in a multistep reaction mechanism that serves as the kinetic bottleneck and dictates the overall rate law; catalysts speed reactions by introducing an alternate lower-Ea pathway.

Heat exchanged between a chemical system and its surroundings at constant pressure (ΔHrxn); negative values denote exothermic heat release to the surroundings and positive values denote endothermic heat absorption.

Experimental method for quantifying heat flow in a chemical or physical change via q = mcΔT, applying energy conservation so heat lost by the system equals heat gained by the solution (qsys = -qsurr).

occurrences.sectionHeading: Calorimetry and the energy of phase changes

glossary.definition: Thermochemical principle stating that because enthalpy is a path-independent state function, the overall ΔH°rxn equals the algebraic sum of ΔH° values for any set of steps summing to the target equation.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Enthalpy of reaction: bond enthalpies, formation, and Hess’s law

glossary.definition: Predictive rule stating that if a system at dynamic equilibrium is disturbed by changing concentration, partial pressure, volume, or temperature, the reaction shifts in the direction that partially opposes the stress.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Dynamic equilibrium and response to stress

glossary.definition: Instantaneous product-to-reactant ratio (Q) written identically to the equilibrium expression K; comparing Q to K predicts shift direction (Q < K proceeds forward, Q > K reverses, and Q = K at equilibrium).

occurrences.sectionHeading: Calculating and interpreting the equilibrium constant

glossary.definition: Reduction in the molar solubility of a sparingly soluble ionic salt when dissolved in a solution already containing one of its constituent ions, shifting the Ksp equilibrium back toward solid precipitate.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Solubility equilibria and the common-ion effect

glossary.definition: Acid-base pair differing by a single proton (H+): the acid donates H+ to generate its conjugate base, while the base accepts H+ to form its conjugate acid, with stronger acids paired to weaker conjugate bases.
Stage in a weak acid–strong base titration where half of the weak acid has been neutralized, making [HA] = [A-] so that pH equals pKa and the solution exhibits optimal buffering against pH shifts.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Acid-base titrations and the molecular structure of acids

glossary.definition: Quantitative capacity of a conjugate weak acid-base buffer to resist pH changes upon adding strong acid or base; increases with higher absolute concentrations of both buffer components near pH = pKa.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Buffers: pKa, Henderson-Hasselbalch, capacity, and solubility

glossary.definition: Thermodynamic state function (ΔG° = ΔH° - TΔS°) predicting reaction favorability at constant temperature and pressure; ΔG° < 0 denotes a product-favored process (K > 1) whereas ΔG° > 0 is reactant-favored.
Tendency of a chemical process to proceed spontaneously toward products (ΔG° < 0, K > 1, E°cell > 0); independent of reaction rate, since a favored reaction may still be slow under kinetic control.

occurrences.sectionHeading: Free energy, equilibrium, and coupled reactions

glossary.definition: Thermodynamically favored electrochemical cell (E°cell > 0, ΔG° < 0) where oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode drive electrons through an external wire while a salt bridge preserves electroneutrality.

quickReference.title: Moles, Mass Spec, PES & Periodic Trends
quickReference.purpose: Grounds stoichiometric mass-mole conversions, isotopic abundance math, photoelectron spectroscopy reading, and Coulombic explanations of periodic trends.
checklist: Convert all sample masses or percentages into moles before comparing atom ratios or determining empirical formulas.
Read photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) x-axis orientation carefully because binding energy often runs high-to-low from left to right.
Justify periodic trends using nuclear charge (Zeff), energy level/shielding shells (n), and distance in Coulomb's law rather than citing a trend direction alone.
formulas: Mole relations: n = m / M and N = n × NA, where Avogadro's constant NA = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Average atomic mass = Σ(isotopic mass × fractional abundance); molecular formula multiplier = molar mass / empirical formula mass.
Coulomb's law attraction: F ∝ (q1·q2) / r²; higher Zeff or smaller shell distance r increases binding energy and first ionization energy.
Electron configuration order follows Aufbau, Hund's rule, and Pauli exclusion; transition-metal cations lose outer ns electrons before (n − 1)d electrons.
decisionRules: When you see a PES spectrum with peak heights in a 2:2:6:2:3 ratio → assign 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³ (phosphorus) from highest to lowest binding energy.
When you see a huge jump between the 2nd and 3rd successive ionization energies → conclude the element has 2 valence electrons (Group 2) and the 3rd removes a core electron.
When you see first ionization energy dip slightly from Group 15 (N/P) to Group 16 (O/S) → explain electron-electron repulsion in the first paired p orbital.
When you see an isoelectronic series (such as O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺) → rank radius smallest for the ion with the greatest nuclear charge (most protons).
cautions: Never justify a periodic trend on an AP FRQ by saying "it is further right on the periodic table"; always cite effective nuclear charge, shell count, and Coulombic attraction.
In a mass spectrum, peak height/area gives relative isotopic abundance, not the number of valence electrons.
Ionization of Fe ([Ar] 4s² 3d⁶) to Fe²⁺ removes the 4s electrons first to give [Ar] 3d⁶, not 4s² 3d⁴.

quickReference.title: Bonding, Lattice Energy, Lewis & VSEPR Geometry
quickReference.purpose: Connects ionic vs. covalent bond energy models with formal-charge Lewis selection, resonance bond orders, hybridization, and molecular polarity.
checklist: Sum total valence electrons accurately (adding for anions, subtracting for cations) before placing bonds and lone pairs.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry (counts lone pairs + bonding regions) from molecular geometry (atoms only) before stating bond angles.
Evaluate molecular polarity by combining individual bond dipoles with 3D molecular symmetry rather than bond electronegativity alone.
formulas: Formal charge: FC = (valence e⁻) − (nonbonding e⁻) − (½ × bonding e⁻); best Lewis structure minimizes |FC| and places negative FC on the most electronegative atom.
Lattice energy: |U| ∝ |q1·q2| / (r_cation + r_anion); higher ionic charges dominate first, then smaller ionic radii increase melting point.
Resonance bond order = (total bonding pairs across equivalent bonds) / (number of bond locations); single = 1σ, double = 1σ + 1π, triple = 1σ + 2π.
Hybridization from steric number (bonded atoms + lone pairs): 2 → sp (180°), 3 → sp² (120°), 4 → sp³ (109.5°; lone pairs compress angles to ~107° or ~104.5°).
decisionRules: When you see a potential-energy vs. internuclear-distance curve → read the minimum x-value as equilibrium bond length and depth below zero as bond dissociation energy.
When you see two ionic solids like MgO and NaF with similar internuclear distances → pick MgO for much higher melting point because (+2)(−2) quadruples the charge product.
When you see equivalent resonance forms (such as CO3²⁻ or NO3⁻) → state that all C-O or N-O bonds have equal intermediate length and strength, not flipping single/double bonds.
When you see a central atom with polar bonds arranged symmetrically (CO2, BF3, CF4, SF6) → conclude bond dipoles cancel and the overall molecule is nonpolar.
cautions: AP Chemistry explicitly excludes sp³d and sp³d² hybridization for expanded octets; identify VSEPR geometry only for 5- and 6-domain species.
Interstitial alloys insert small atoms (like C in steel) into lattice holes to stiffen the metal, whereas substitutional alloys swap similarly sized metal atoms (like brass).
Covalent bonds break only during chemical reactions, not when molecular substances melt or boil.

quickReference.title: IMFs, Gases, Solutions & Spectroscopy
quickReference.purpose: Links intermolecular attractions to phase properties and separations while organizing gas laws, molarity, and spectroscopic Beer-Lambert analysis.
checklist: Match gas constant R units to pressure and volume (0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) vs. 62.36 L·torr/(mol·K)) and always convert Celsius to Kelvin.
Identify the bonding class (molecular, ionic, metallic, covalent network) before comparing boiling or melting points.
Verify cuvette wavelength matches λmax and absorbance stays in the linear calibration region when applying Beer-Lambert law.
formulas: Ideal Gas Law & Mixtures: PV = nRT; Dalton's Law P_total = ΣP_i and P_i = X_i·P_total; molar mass from gas density M = dRT / P.
Kinetic Molecular Theory: KE_avg = (3/2)RT depends only on Kelvin temperature; lighter gases move faster (u_rms ∝ √(T/M)) at the same T.
Solution concentration & dilution: M = mol solute / L solution and M1V1 = M2V2 (conserves moles of solute).
Spectroscopy: E = hν = hc / λ (h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s); Beer-Lambert Law A = εbc (absorbance proportional to concentration).
decisionRules: When you see two nonpolar molecules with very different boiling points (such as I2 vs. F2) → explain higher boiling point via larger electron cloud, greater polarizability, and stronger London dispersion forces.
When you see a real gas deviating below ideal PV/nRT at low temperature and moderate pressure → attribute the dip to intermolecular attractions reducing wall-collision force.
When you see UV-Vis spectroscopy vs. IR vs. microwave spectra → match UV-Vis to electronic transitions, IR to bond vibrations, and microwave to molecular rotations.

When you see a paper chromatography spot traveling close to a nonpolar solvent front → conclude that component is less polar and interacts more strongly with the mobile phase than the polar stationary phase.
cautions: Hydrogen bonding requires H covalently bonded directly to F, O, or N (not merely an H atom anywhere in a molecule containing O, like dimethyl ether).
All molecules exhibit London dispersion forces; large nonpolar molecules can have stronger total LDFs than small polar or H-bonding molecules.
Rinsing a cuvette with deionized water instead of the sample solution dilutes the sample and lowers measured absorbance A.

quickReference.title: Net Ionic Equations, Stoichiometry & Redox
quickReference.purpose: Structures balanced net ionic writing, limiting-reactant mole accounting, gravimetric/titration assays, and oxidation-reduction half-reactions.
checklist: Write the balanced molecular equation and dissociate only strong electrolytes (aqueous strong acids, strong bases, soluble salts) before canceling spectators.
Compare mole ratios of all reactants against stoichiometric coefficients to confirm the limiting reactant before predicting product yield.
Verify both atom balance and total electric charge balance in every net ionic and redox half-reaction.
formulas: Solubility guarantee rule: all sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), ammonium (NH4+), and nitrate (NO3−) salts are soluble in water.
Percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%; percent error = (|measured − accepted| / accepted) × 100%.
Titration stoichiometry at equivalence: (mol analyte / coeff_analyte) = (mol titrant / coeff_titrant), with mol = M × V(L).
Redox tracking: oxidation increases oxidation number (loses electrons at anode); reduction decreases oxidation number (gains electrons at cathode); balance O with H2O and H with H+ in acid.
decisionRules: When you see a precipitation reaction producing a white solid after mixing two aqueous salts → eliminate soluble spectator ions (such as Na+ and NO3−) and keep only the ions forming the solid.
When you see a weak acid reacting with a strong base in a net ionic equation → keep the weak acid molecular (HA) on the reactant side and show OH− producing A− and H2O.
When you see a gravimetric precipitate weighed before being completely dried → predict an artificially high calculated mass percent of the target ion.
When you see an element's oxidation state change from reactant to product (such as MnO4− to Mn2+) → classify as redox rather than acid-base or precipitation.
cautions: Do not split weak acids (like HF or CH3COOH), solids, liquids, or gases into ions in a net ionic equation.
The reactant with the smaller starting mass is not necessarily the limiting reactant; always compare moles divided by stoichiometric coefficients.
In basic redox balancing, finish balancing in acidic solution first, then add equal OH− to both sides to neutralize H+ into H2O.

quickReference.title: Rate Laws, Integrated Plots & Reaction Mechanisms
quickReference.purpose: Links experimental initial-rate tables, linearized concentration-time plots, collision theory, and multistep mechanism validation.
checklist: Never infer reaction order directly from overall balanced equation coefficients; read exponents from experimental data or an elementary step.
Check which integrated plot (Concentration vs. t, ln[A] vs. t, or 1/[A] vs. t) produces a straight line before assigning order and slope sign.
Confirm that proposed elementary steps sum to the overall balanced reaction and that no intermediate appears in the final derived rate law.
formulas: Relative rate for aA + bB → cC: Rate = −(1/a)(Δ[A]/Δt) = −(1/b)(Δ[B]/Δt) = +(1/c)(Δ[C]/Δt).
Integrated rate laws: 0th order [A]t − [A]0 = −kt; 1st order ln[A]t − ln[A]0 = −kt (constant half-life t1/2 = 0.693 / k); 2nd order 1/[A]t − 1/[A]0 = +kt.
Rate constant units for overall order n: k has units M^(1−n)·s⁻¹ (0th: M·s⁻¹, 1st: s⁻¹, 2nd: M⁻¹·s⁻¹).
Collision model & catalysis: rate depends on collision frequency, proper orientation, and fraction exceeding Ea (k = A·e^(−Ea/RT)); catalysts lower Ea via an alternate pathway.
decisionRules: When you see concentration double while initial rate quadruples (holding other reactants constant) → assign 2nd order with respect to that reactant.
When you see half-life remain identical across successive 50% drops in concentration → identify 1st-order kinetics and compute k = 0.693 / t1/2.
When you see a slow step following a fast reversible equilibrium step → write the slow-step rate law and substitute the intermediate using the fast-step equilibrium expression.
When you see a species consumed in step 1 and regenerated in a later step → identify it as a catalyst, whereas one formed then consumed is a reaction intermediate.
cautions: Raising temperature increases rate constant k primarily because a much larger fraction of molecules exceeds activation energy Ea, not merely because collisions are slightly more frequent.
A catalyst lowers activation energy Ea for both forward and reverse steps equally without changing overall ΔH or ΔG.
For a 2nd-order reaction, plotting 1/[A] vs. t has a positive slope (+k), whereas 0th and 1st order linear plots have negative slopes (−k).

quickReference.title: Calorimetry, Phase Changes, Hess's Law & Bond Enthalpy
quickReference.purpose: Organizes sign conventions for heat transfer, coffee-cup calorimetry calculations, phase-transition plateaus, and three independent paths to ΔH°rxn.
checklist: Verify system vs. surroundings signs: if solution temperature rises, q_solution is positive and q_rxn = −q_solution is negative (exothermic).
Convert joules from q = mcΔT to kilojoules and divide by moles of the limiting reactant (per reaction stoichiometry) to report ΔHrxn in kJ/mol_rxn.
Check the formula direction: products minus reactants for ΔH°f, but bonds broken (reactants) minus bonds formed (products) for bond enthalpies.
formulas: Sensible heat & calorimetry: q = m·c·ΔT (water c = 4.184 J/(g·°C)); constant-pressure calorimetry ΔH_rxn = −q_soln / n_rxn.
Phase transitions at constant temperature: q = n·ΔH_fus (melting/freezing) or q = n·ΔH_vap (vaporizing/condensing); sum heating segments separately.
Standard enthalpies of formation: ΔH°_rxn = Σ[n·ΔH°_f(products)] − Σ[m·ΔH°_f(reactants)]; ΔH°_f = 0 for elements in their standard reference states.
Bond enthalpy approximation: ΔH_rxn ≈ Σ(D_bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(D_bonds formed in products); breaking bonds is endothermic (+), forming bonds is exothermic (−).
decisionRules: When you see a heating curve plateau where added heat produces zero temperature rise → recognize potential energy increasing to overcome intermolecular forces during a phase change.
When you see Hess's Law steps that must be reversed or scaled → flip the sign of ΔH when reversing an equation and multiply ΔH by the same scaling factor.
When you see a reaction releasing heat because product bonds are stronger than reactant bonds → predict a negative ΔH_rxn (exothermic).
When you see heat escaping from an uninsulated coffee-cup calorimeter during an exothermic dissolution → conclude the measured |ΔT| and calculated |ΔH| will be smaller than the true value.
cautions: In aqueous solution calorimetry, mass m in q = mcΔT is the total mass of the combined solution (solute + solvent), not just the limiting reactant mass.
Breaking chemical bonds ALWAYS requires energy input (endothermic); energy is released when new bonds form, never when bonds break.
Bond-enthalpy calculations give approximate gas-phase ΔH values because tabulated bond energies are averages across different molecules.

quickReference.title: K, Q, Le Châtelier & Solubility Product (Ksp)
quickReference.purpose: Anchors equilibrium expression setup, Q-vs-K reaction-direction proofs, RICE-table math, disturbance analysis, and precipitation equilibria.
checklist: Omit pure solids (s) and pure liquids (l) from Kc, Kp, Q, and Ksp expressions; include only aqueous (aq) and gaseous (g) species.
Distinguish whether a disturbance changes Q at constant K (concentration/volume) or changes the numerical value of K itself (temperature only).
Track stoichiometric exponents carefully when converting between molar solubility s and Ksp (for example, AB2 gives Ksp = 4s³).
formulas: Law of mass action for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: Kc = ([C]^c [D]^d) / ([A]^a [B]^b); Kp uses partial pressures in atm.
Manipulating K: reversing a reaction yields 1/K; multiplying stoichiometry by n yields K^n; adding reactions yields K_net = K1 × K2.
Reaction quotient test: Q less than K → net forward shift; Q equals K → dynamic equilibrium; Q greater than K → net reverse shift.
Solubility equilibrium for M_x X_y(s) ⇌ x M^(y+) + y X^(x−): Ksp = [M^(y+)]^x [X^(x−)]^y; precipitate forms if Qsp exceeds Ksp.
decisionRules: When you see container volume halved at constant temperature → double all gas concentrations/pressures, compute Q vs. K, and shift toward the side with fewer moles of gas.
When you see temperature increased on an exothermic equilibrium (ΔH negative) → treat heat as a product, so K decreases and the reaction shifts toward reactants.
When you see a sparingly soluble salt placed into a solution already containing one of its ions → apply the common-ion effect to predict reduced molar solubility while Ksp stays constant.
When you see Ksp values compared between salts of different stoichiometries (like AgCl vs. Ag2CrO4) → solve for molar solubility s explicitly instead of comparing raw Ksp magnitudes.
cautions: Adding more solid reactant or product never shifts equilibrium and does not alter Q, provided some solid was already present.
Adding an inert gas at constant volume leaves all partial pressures unchanged, so Q stays equal to K with zero shift.
Temperature is the ONLY factor that changes the numerical value of an equilibrium constant K.

quickReference.title: pH, Buffers, Titrations & Molecular Acid Strength
quickReference.purpose: Separates strong vs. weak acid-base stoichiometry, Henderson-Hasselbalch buffer reasoning, titration curve landmarks, and structural pKa trends.
checklist: Classify every acid and base as strong or weak first, and perform stoichiometry in moles before converting back to molarity with the new total volume.
Identify the titration zone (initial, buffer region, half-equivalence, equivalence, or excess titrant) before choosing an equilibrium equation.
Check temperature when using pH + pOH = 14, because Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ applies strictly at 25 °C.
formulas: Water autoionization & conjugates (25 °C): Kw = [H3O+][OH−] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, pH = −log[H3O+], pH + pOH = 14, and Ka × Kb = Kw.
Henderson-Hasselbalch buffer equation: pH = pKa + log([A−] / [HA]); optimal buffer range is pKa ± 1, with capacity increasing at higher conjugate concentrations.
Titration landmarks for weak acid HA + strong base OH−: at half-equivalence [HA] = [A−] so pH = pKa; at equivalence only weak base A− remains so pH exceeds 7.
Acid strength structure rules: binary acids strengthen down a group (weaker H-X bond) and across a period (more polar); oxyacids strengthen with more O atoms or more electronegative central atom.
decisionRules: When you see [A−] exceeding [HA] in a buffer or indicator solution → immediately determine that pH is greater than pKa (and vice versa when [HA] exceeds [A−]).
When you see a weak base titrated with a strong acid → expect the equivalence point pH to be below 7 because the conjugate acid BH+ hydrolyzes water.
When you see a pH indicator selection prompt → choose an indicator whose pKa sits closest to the equivalence point pH of the titration.
When you see equal volumes of 0.10 M HCl and 0.10 M CH3COOH titrated with 0.10 M NaOH → recognize both require the exact same volume of NaOH to reach equivalence.
cautions: Strong acids and bases (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4 first proton, HClO4; Group 1 and heavy Group 2 hydroxides) ionize ~100% and do not use ICE tables.
At higher temperatures where Kw exceeds 10⁻¹⁴, pure neutral water has pH below 7 yet remains strictly neutral because [H3O+] still equals [OH−].
Adding water to dilute a buffer keeps the [A−]/[HA] ratio unchanged (pH nearly constant) while reducing its buffer capacity.

quickReference.title: Entropy, Gibbs Free Energy & Electrochemical Cells
quickReference.purpose: Unifies spontaneity criteria across ΔG°, K, and E°cell alongside galvanic vs. electrolytic cell operation, Nernst shifts, and Faraday electrolysis.
checklist: Reconcile energy units before computing ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° by converting ΔS° from J/(mol·K) to kJ/(mol·K) and T to Kelvin.
Verify standard reduction potentials are NOT multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients when computing E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.
Confirm electron flow (anode → cathode externally) and ion migration in the salt bridge (anions → anode, cations → cathode) match cell type.
formulas: Gibbs free energy & spontaneity: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and ΔG° = −RT ln K (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K)); thermodynamically favored when ΔG° negative, K greater than 1, and E°cell positive.
Cell potential & work: E°cell = E°red(cathode) − E°red(anode); ΔG° = −nFE°cell where F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻ and 1 V = 1 J/C.
Nonstandard cell potential (Nernst): Ecell = E°cell − (RT / nF) ln Q; raising reactant concentration lowers Q and increases Ecell.
Faraday electrolysis stoichiometry: q = I·t (coulombs = amperes × seconds), mol e⁻ = (I·t) / F, and mass deposited = (mol e⁻ / n) × molar mass.
decisionRules: When you see ΔH° positive and ΔS° positive → conclude the reaction is thermodynamically favored only at high temperatures where TΔS° exceeds ΔH°.
When you see a thermodynamically favored reaction (ΔG° strongly negative) proceeding undetectably slowly → cite kinetic control caused by a large activation energy Ea.
When you see an electrochemical cell with E°cell negative → classify it as nonspontaneous and require an external power source (electrolytic cell) to drive it.
When you see a galvanic cell running until it reaches equilibrium ("dead battery") → set Q = K and Ecell = 0 V.
cautions: Never multiply E°red values when balancing half-reactions; cell potential is an intensive ratio of joules per coulomb.
In both galvanic and electrolytic cells, oxidation ALWAYS occurs at the anode (AN OX) and reduction ALWAYS occurs at the cathode (RED CAT).
Watch the factor of 1000 between joules (from R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) or F = 96,485 C/mol) and kilojoules reported for ΔG° and ΔH°.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Stoichiometry and Limiting Reactant Mass Shortcut
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners identify the limiting reactant by choosing the smaller given mass or smaller raw mole amount without dividing by balanced stoichiometric coefficients, or calculate product yield from the excess reactant.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Convert every reactant to moles, divide each by its balanced coefficient to find reaction extents, and run a Before-Change-After (BCA) mole table to track both product formed and excess remaining.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Intermolecular Forces vs. Intramolecular Covalent Bonds
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners claim phase changes like boiling or melting break covalent bonds inside molecules, misattribute hydrogen bonding to molecules lacking N−H, O−H, or F−H bonds, or ignore polarizability in London dispersion forces.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Separate substance type first (molecular vs. ionic vs. covalent network vs. metallic), identify the exact attraction broken during phase change, and verify H-bond donor/acceptor atoms before ranking boiling points.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Reaction Quotient (Q) vs. Equilibrium Constant (K) Shift Confusion
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners include pure solids or liquids in Q and K expressions, predict that concentration or pressure changes alter the numerical value of K, or invert the shift direction when Q exceeds K.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Write Q using only aqueous and gaseous species, compare Q against K to predict the forward or reverse shift, and enforce the rule that only a temperature change modifies K.

misconceptionFamilies.label: pH, Equivalence Point, and Buffer Henderson-Hasselbalch Trap
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners assume every titration reaches equivalence at pH 7.00, confuse the half-equivalence buffer point (pH = pKa) with equivalence, or plug pre-neutralization molarities into Henderson-Hasselbalch without doing stoichiometry first.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Run a mole-based neutralization table before any equilibrium step, identify the dominant species left in solution (buffer pair vs. weak conjugate salt vs. excess strong species), and match the pH method to that regime.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Kinetics vs. Thermodynamics Conflation
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners assume a reaction with negative ΔG° must proceed quickly, claim a catalyst alters ΔH° or equilibrium yield, or write rate laws from overall stoichiometric coefficients instead of experimental orders or the rate-determining step.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Partition every reaction-coordinate problem into two separate questions: barrier height Ea and slow-step molecularity (kinetics) versus reactant-to-product energy gap ΔH° and ΔG° (thermodynamics).

misconceptionFamilies.label: Sign Convention Reversals in ΔH°, ΔG°, and E°cell
misconceptionFamilies.description: Learners flip endothermic/exothermic signs in bond-enthalpy sums (reactants − products vs. products − reactants), mix J and kJ in ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°, or multiply standard reduction potentials E° by stoichiometric coefficients.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Verify sign polarity and units before computing: bond breaking is positive and bond forming is negative; convert ΔS° to kJ/(mol·K); keep intensive E° values unscaled and check ΔG° = −nFE°cell sign alignment.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Stoichiometry and Limiting Reactant Mass Shortcut
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Using Reaction-Extent Ratios and BCA Tables for Limiting Reactants
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You picked the limiting reactant by comparing raw grams or unscaled moles, or reported zero leftover reactant for the species that actually stayed in excess.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: When you divide each reactant mole amount by its balanced stoichiometric coefficient, which reactant allows the fewest full reaction turnovers?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Compare your original choice against the balanced equation and highlight where molar mass or stoichiometric ratio (such as 2:1 or 3:2) overturned the raw mass comparison.
stages.requiredOutput: A short diagnostic line showing raw grams, raw moles, and mole-to-coefficient ratios for every reactant.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Build a 3-row Before-Change-After (BCA) mole table using the smaller reaction extent x so the limiting reactant hits 0 mol while excess reactant and products update in strict stoichiometric multiples of x.
stages.requiredOutput: A complete BCA mole table with final moles of product produced and final moles (and grams) of excess reactant remaining.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Solve a particulate-diagram stoichiometry item and a precipitation molarity limiting-reactant item by counting stoichiometric packets rather than raw particle totals.
stages.requiredOutput: Two verified counts showing remaining spectator/excess particles and theoretical yield in moles.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the missed Unit 4 item and a percent-yield transfer item where experimental yield is compared against the limiting-reactant theoretical yield.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct final answers on both items with explicit identification of the limiting reactant and the BCA extent x.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Intermolecular Forces vs. Intramolecular Covalent Bonds
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Distinguishing Intermolecular Attractions from Covalent Bonds
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You explained a higher boiling point by citing stronger C−H or O−H covalent bonds inside the molecule, or claimed hydrogen bonding exists in a molecule where H is bonded only to carbon.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: During vaporization of this substance, do intact molecules separate from each other by overcoming IMFs, or is this a covalent network solid whose actual covalent bonds break?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Draw two neighboring molecules of the substance in the prompt and label the intramolecular bonds inside one molecule separately from the dashed intermolecular attractions between the two molecules.
stages.requiredOutput: A two-molecule sketch or text diagram distinguishing intact intramolecular bonds from broken intermolecular attractions during boiling.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Inventory all IMFs for both compared substances (London dispersion scaled by electron cloud size/polarizability, dipole-dipole, and true H-bonding requiring H covalently attached to N, O, or F).
stages.requiredOutput: A side-by-side IMF checklist naming the decisive interaction that accounts for the higher boiling point or lower vapor pressure.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Rank two AP Chem trap pairs: CH₃OCH₃ vs. CH₃CH₂OH (isomers testing H-bonding) and F₂ vs. I₂ (nonpolar halogens where larger electron cloud polarizability drives higher boiling point).
stages.requiredOutput: Two AP FRQ-ready justification sentences naming both substances, their specific IMFs, and why one requires more thermal energy to separate.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the missed Unit 2/3 item and a new solubility or chromatography polarity item without once conflating covalent bond strength with IMF strength.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct selections on both items accompanied by an explicit check of whether molecules stay intact during the physical change.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Reaction Quotient (Q) vs. Equilibrium Constant (K) Shift Confusion
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Diagnosing Equilibrium Shifts via Q vs. K Without Mutating K
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You predicted a shift after adding a pure solid, claimed adding reactant increases K, or moved the reaction forward even though Q already exceeded K.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: How does the disturbance immediately change the numerator or denominator of Q (using only aqueous and gaseous terms), and did the temperature change at all?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Write the exact mass-action expression Q for the reaction in the stem, crossing out any pure solid (s) or liquid (l), and note where your previous answer mistakenly changed K or included a solid.
stages.requiredOutput: The cleaned Q expression alongside a one-line diagnosis of the original Le Chatelier or K-invariance slip.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Apply the Q-vs-K compass: if Q is smaller than K, the system shifts right (products increase) until Q = K; if Q exceeds K, the system shifts left (reactants increase) until Q = K; only temperature moves K.
stages.requiredOutput: A completed disturbance table showing immediate effect on Q, comparison of Q against K, shift direction, and whether K stayed constant or changed.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Evaluate three classic AP Equilibrium perturbations on an exothermic gas reaction: halving container volume, adding inert He gas at constant volume, and raising temperature.
stages.requiredOutput: Three concise verdicts giving the Q-vs-K relation, shift direction, and K status (unchanged vs. decreased) for each perturbation.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the missed Unit 7 item and solve a solubility-equilibrium (Ksp) common-ion item using the same Q-vs-K framework.
stages.requiredOutput: Verified correct answers on both items showing why adding a common ion makes Q exceed Ksp without changing Ksp.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: pH, Equivalence Point, and Buffer Henderson-Hasselbalch Trap
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Separating Stoichiometric Neutralization from Buffer and Salt Hydrolysis
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You set the weak-acid/strong-base equivalence point to pH 7.00, used pH = pKa at equivalence instead of half-equivalence, or ignored the stoichiometry of added strong base.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: After the one-way neutralization reaction finishes in moles, which acid-base species actually remain in the flask?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Locate the titration point in the missed item on a weak-acid/strong-base curve (initial, buffer region, half-equivalence, equivalence, or post-equivalence) and note which zone rule you misapplied.
stages.requiredOutput: Zone label for the item plus the exact mismatch (for instance, applying neutral pH 7.00 where conjugate base A⁻ hydrolyzes to produce OH⁻).

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Execute the two-step AP Acid-Base protocol: Step 1 complete a mole BCA neutralization table; Step 2 choose the matching equilibrium equation (Henderson-Hasselbalch if both HA and A⁻ remain; Kb hydrolysis if only A⁻ remains; excess OH⁻ molarity if strong base dominates).
stages.requiredOutput: Completed mole BCA table followed by the regime-matched pH setup and qualitative check (basic equivalence pH for weak acid + strong base).

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Compare the pH and buffer capacity of two acetate buffers: one at 0.10 M HA / 0.10 M A⁻ and one at 0.50 M HA / 0.50 M A⁻, then predict how adding 0.02 mol HCl shifts the [A⁻]/[HA] ratio.
stages.requiredOutput: Explanation showing both share pH = pKa initially, why the 0.50 M buffer resists pH drift more strongly, and the updated mole ratio after HCl addition.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the missed Unit 8 item and transfer the protocol to a weak-base/strong-acid titration curve item asking for the best indicator or dominant species at a given pH.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct choices on both items with explicit identification of the dominant species (BH⁺ vs. B) relative to pKa.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Decoupling Activation Energy and Rate Laws from ΔG° and ΔH°
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You predicted a faster reaction solely because ΔG° was very negative, claimed a catalyst lowers ΔH° or shifts K, or copied overall equation coefficients into the rate law.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does the prompt ask about the pathway barrier and reaction speed (kinetics: Ea, k, slow step) or the endpoint stability and yield (thermodynamics: ΔH°, ΔG°, K)?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Sort every term in the missed Unit 5 item into two buckets: Kinetics (rate, k, Ea, half-life, slow step, catalyst pathway) versus Thermodynamics (ΔH°, ΔS°, ΔG°, K), flagging where your answer crossed the boundary.
stages.requiredOutput: A two-bucket classification identifying the exact kinetics-thermodynamics crossover error.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Inspect a reaction-coordinate diagram with and without a catalyst, marking that a catalyst introduces an alternate mechanism with lower Ea while leaving reactant energy, product energy, ΔH°, and K untouched.
stages.requiredOutput: An annotated energy-profile summary contrasting what changes with a catalyst (Ea, k, mechanism steps) against what stays invariant (ΔH°, ΔG°, K).

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Determine the rate law for a two-step mechanism (fast equilibrium followed by slow second step) and verify why an intermediate must be substituted out using the fast pre-equilibrium.
stages.requiredOutput: The derived experimental rate law expressed solely in terms of reactants (no intermediate) plus a check confirming it differs from the overall stoichiometry.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-attempt the missed kinetics item and solve a thermodynamically favorable yet kinetically controlled reaction prompt (such as diamond → graphite or H₂O₂ decomposition).
stages.requiredOutput: Correct responses on both items clearly separating high activation barrier from negative ΔG°.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Sign Convention Reversals in ΔH°, ΔG°, and E°cell
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Enforcing Sign, Unit, and Intensive-Property Discipline in Thermo & Electrochem
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: You subtracted reactants from products in a bond-enthalpy sum, forgot to divide ΔS° by 1000 before subtracting TΔS°, or doubled E° when doubling a half-reaction.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does your final sign make physical sense across all three linked indicators: exothermic/endothermic heat flow, ΔG° negativity, and positive E°cell for a galvanic cell?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Audit your calculation from the missed Unit 6 or Unit 9 item against three red-flag checkpoints: formula direction (broken − formed vs. ΔHf° products − reactants), J-to-kJ unit match, and intensive E° invariance.
stages.requiredOutput: A specific tag naming which of the three sign/unit traps inverted the original answer.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Assemble a unified favorability alignment strip: thermodynamically favorable ↔ ΔG° negative ↔ K greater than 1 ↔ E°cell positive (via ΔG° = −nFE°cell = −RT ln K).
stages.requiredOutput: A completed alignment table verifying consistent signs across ΔH°, ΔS° (in kJ/mol·K), ΔG°, K, and E°cell for the prompt reaction.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Work two precision drills: compute ΔH°rxn from bond energies (sum broken − sum formed) and compute E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode for a 2e⁻/3e⁻ redox reaction without scaling either reduction potential.
stages.requiredOutput: Two sign-verified calculations showing explicit unit conversion and confirming n = 6 enters ΔG° = −nFE°cell while E°cell remains unscaled.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the original Unit 6/9 item and one temperature-dependence item predicting when a reaction with ΔH° positive and ΔS° positive switches from non-spontaneous to spontaneous.
stages.requiredOutput: Correct solutions on both items including the threshold temperature estimate T = ΔH° / ΔS° with matching energy units.
